articles.title: James has knee surgery; Martínez sorry; Watford sacking reports ‘fake news’: football – live

Right, I’m going to step away from the blog for a while. I leave you in the capable hands of Luke McLaughlin, who you can email here if you fancy. Back in a bit!

Despite reports suggesting he would be sacked if Watford lost at Cardiff on Tuesday, Alessio Dionisi remains in post. “There is good news, bad news or fake news probably,” the Italian told the BBC yesterday. “In this case for the moment, it is fake news. But I don’t decide.”

The situation at the club is dire: a squad haphazardly thrown together, with no money spent on transfer fees in the summer, the division’s lowest wage bill, few players arriving until the final days of the window, a miserable dearth of Championship experience (which the club leadership acknowledged and pledged to address at the end of last season, and for that matter before most recent transfer windows), a disjointed and lopsided squad notably bereft of midfield options, and an aloof and increasingly unpopular owner.

Since the start of March the club have played 21 league games and won only three, the worst record of any club which has been in the division throughout that time (indeed Coventry, Ipswich, West Ham and Oxford United all have more wins and more Championship points despite spending much of it in other divisions). Most recently they played Burnley at home when their opponents were bottom of the league and lost 4-0, and then went to 21st-placed Cardiff and lost 5-1. They are now 22nd, and both Elton John – who said he was “upset and disappointed at the decline” – and Troy Deeney have criticised the way they are playing and the way they are being run.

Today Gino Pozzo is meeting a representative of fans’ group the 1881 Movement – who recently published an open letter stating their “complete loss of confidence” in Pozzo, and criticising “the endless cycle of appointments and dismissals [which] has reduced a once-proud club to a source of ridicule”. Tomorrow they host 13th-placed but also troubled Charlton, who won three of their first four league games but have not secured a victory since August.

Word is that the club has already made contact with potential replacements for Dionisi, but that the level of vitriol coming from those fans still sufficiently motivated to turn up to games has stayed Pozzo’s hand, for now. The club certainly have some players, the likes of Othmane Maamma and Myron Boadu, who are able to play at a much higher level to the one the team is currently showing, but do they have the motivation (and the teammates) to demonstrate that ability, or has the cycle of sackings drained the squad of all motivation and cohesion?

Coventry boss Frank Lampard is not prepared to relax after watching his side record back-to-back wins in the Premier League , writes the Press Association .

The Sky Blues looked to be in for a long season after losing their opening four games without scoring a goal. But they have kick-started their campaign with wins against Nottingham Forest and Newcastle and as he prepares to visit Tottenham on Monday Lampard wants to keep the foot on the gas.

“Keep driving it,” he said. “It’s very important to look at the the good things out of the game, also the things we can improve. But when we talk about the good things, I’m not overly patting them on the back because we have to work hard to get better.

“Every game brings different challenges, so I think the players understand me and my approach and the staff’s approach here. We never want to rest. I don’t. I’m always fearful of resting on something and thinking that you’ve made it. This league’s too difficult for that.

“So one of my first jobs is to keep pushing from that front, and the players need to feel that.”

Sky are reporting that Reece James, who Chelsea confirmed this morning had undergone minor knee surgery, is expected to be out for three months.

Fulham fans fretting about life under Álvaro Arbeloa will not feel any better when they remember how things were under Marco Silva, who was one of the most effective managers in the Premier League when it came to making substitutions.

Silva’s substitutes were involved in the fourth-highest goal contributions last season and the most in the 2024-25 season. Fulham knew how to dig in and salvage unlikely points. But Silva left last summer, joining Benfica after concluding he could achieve nothing more at Craven Cottage, and his replacement is already under pressure after some puzzling tactical choices.

The worrying shift under Arbeloa was evident during Fulham’s collapse against Ipswich last weekend. The west Londoners were 1-0 up and looking good for their first league win of the season when Arbeloa weakened his midfield by replacing Shea Charles with Manuel Ángel in the 70th minute.

It was a strange way to shut up shop. Charles is physically imposing, has impressed since joining from Southampton and was doing well alongside Sander Berge. The 22-year-old Ángel is 5ft 7in, was making his Premier League debut and has little experience of senior football. Ipswich’s comeback to win 2-1 was not a surprise, particularly when Arbeloa’s other rejigs included bringing on Rodrigo Muniz and switching from a 4-2-3-1 system to a flat 4-4-2 in an attempt to defend the lead.

Can you name the three teams still without a win in this season’s Premier League ? If so, you’re approximately 6.7% of the way to full marks in the sports quiz of the week!

Fulham’s Alvaro Arbeloa has held his press conference ahead of tomorrow’s home game against Hull, and has been quizzed on how confident he is that he will still be at the club in a week’s time if they are not able to win:

I am focused on tomorrow’s game, on my players, on my team, that is the most important thing. It’s not about me, it’s about the club, it’s about the players, it’s about the supporters. For me it’s been a normal week. We’ve been working hard. We were preparing for a difficult match against a very difficult team.

I saw the commitment of the players this week, how they have been training. They are so focused on tomorrow’s game. I saw them, how they can play. For me it is the most important thing, the performance of the players. It’s not about my future, it’s about the club and about the players. They are looking for their reward, and looking for a game where they can get a win for our supporters and I think they deserve it.

Donald Trump is likely to end up as the only political leader awarded the Fifa peace prize after Gianni Infantino was told at Thursday’s meeting of Fifa council to make major changes or scrap the controversial award.

The Guardian has learned that several council members demanded the award be abolished and others called for the prize to be depoliticised, with Fifa’s football social responsibility committee to make a recommendation before the next council meeting in Doha on 16 December.

The Women’s Super League table is taking shape for 2026-27. The defending champions, Manchester City, have five wins from five games but more intriguing stories lie elsewhere. Why are Arsenal struggling, who is performing better than results suggest, and in which way are two promoted teams smashing expectations? Andrew Beasley has the answers:

Chelsea have announced that Reece James has had “successful” and “minor” surgery on a knee injury sustained in training. “Reece has already begun his road to recovery and will be supported by the club’s medical department at Cobham during this rehabilitation phase,” the club wrote on social media.

Newcastle head coach Matthias Jaissle says he is uninterested in dwelling on what might have been when highly-rated Aston Villa midfielder Johan Manzambi visits St James’ Park this weekend, writes the Press Association .

Manzambi looked set for a switch to Tyneside over the summer but the deal was hijacked as Villa swooped in to sign the Switzerland international, who has flourished during his short time in the midlands.

The 21-year-old opened the scoring in Villa’s 6-0 Champions League rout of Fenerbahce in midweek and he could rub salt into his former suitors’ wounds when Newcastle welcome Unai Emery’s side on Saturday.

But while Jaissle, who succeeded Eddie Howe after Manzambi snubbed a move to the north-east, is a fan of the youngster, the German side-stepped the question of whether he would have liked him in his ranks.

“He is a really good player,” said Jaissle, who will be looking for a response after Monday’s 4-1 loss at Coventry. “But I’m not here to talk now about players, about rumours, about potential signings. The pure focus is on our players. We have many things to do, many things to improve, and that’s the approach to not get distracted by anything else.”

Joelinton is poised for his first start of the season for Newcastle on Saturday while Dan Burn looks set to be on the bench again, with Anthony Elanga and Jacob Ramsey poised to return to light training next week.

Is there a correlation between running more and winning more in the Premier League , I wonder? We have the answer for you! And it is, to summarise, um, kind of but not really but maybe a bit. Read about it, with graphs and everything, here:

Hello world, and happy Friday! Yes, we are all one day closer to finding out if there are any new depths for our teams still to plumb, which is certainly an exciting prospect for my fellow Watford fans. In unusual coincidence news, this Premier League weekend sees all four English teams who were in action in Europe last night play each other on Sunday – Bournemouth v Sunderland, Brighton v Crystal Palace – while the two Scottish teams who played in Europe last night also play each other on Sunday, with Hearts heading to Celtic. Meanwhile table-topping, relegation-bound Manchester City host Ipswich and second-placed Arsenal head to Nottingham Forest, while Fulham and Spurs, like Bournemouth winless in the league this season, seek those magic three points at home to promoted teams, Fulham v Hull on Saturday and Spurs v Coventry on Monday.

But we get the ball rolling with an apology, after Lisandro Martínez begged forgiveness not for what he said about the shambles at Manchester United , but for the fact that the “time and place … perhaps were not the right ones”, which the way I read it is very much a partial climbdown rather than the fulsome version that some are interpreting it as. Anyway, read all about it!

articles.title: Australia 40-0 Samoa: women’s Rugby League World Cup – live reaction
articles.summary: Defending champion Jillaroos too good in opener in Sydney Any thoughts? Get in touch with an email Australia has kicked off and we’re underway! A number of the Samoan players are tearing up during the anthem – what a special moment for them to be able to represent their country on the world stage. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Well, what an opening game for the women’s tournament! While it didn’t have the close scoreline of the men’s opener last night, there was so much heart and passion on the field and some truly incredible defence from Samoa. I’m looking forward to seeing how they build throughout the tournament – they have so much talent and some very smart players – in particular Freedom Crichton Ropati and Destiny Mino-Sinapati – who will only get better as they go on.

The Jillaroos will take a lot out of that game as well – while they’ll be heartened by the strong win, they will want to cut down their error rate, especially when they come up against New Zealand and England. They made 10 errors and conceded five penalties – many of them at crucial times. I wouldn’t be surprised to see coach Jess Skinner look to mix up some combinations and see if that reduces the error rate.

However, they will be pleased with their 519 post-contact metres and nine line breaks – they are always making things happen out on the field and when they can hold on to the ball they will have the chance to score even more tries.

Both teams have a week off now – Samoa will come up against Wales next Friday back at CommBank Stadium, while the Jillaroos take on England in Perth next Saturday.

I hope you enjoyed this great battle tonight and keep on watching the incredible women playing in all the teams at this tournament. Until next time, go rugby league!

One thing that’s great to see is all the babies around this team. Once upon a time, women had to retire from sport if they wanted to have kids. Now they have the opportunity to take time out and come back and play on the world stage with their kids watching from the stands. Millie Elliott’s daughter steals the show by stealing the microphone cover during her interview. It’s such a wonderful thing to see for so many reasons!

“That was really tough,” she says. “I want to congratulate Samoa, they’ve worked really hard and made it really tough for us out there.”

Samoa captain Annetta Nuuausala is equally complimentary of the Australian team.

“We knew coming into this game that they were going to give it to us,” she says. “They’re the pinnacle of women’s rugby league internationally, so we knew it would be tough.”

A well-deserved player of the match award for Jocelyn Kelleher on debut. Her kicking game – both goal kicking and kicking in play – was sensational.

“It was a dream come true, I had so much fun, I loved it,” she says. “All our hard work paid off today.”

Despite what the scoreline says, it truly was a sensational effort from Samoa tonight. Their tryline defence was so strong, but in attack they couldn’t get enough possession and territory to score or hold Australia out every time.

A comprehensive win from the Jillaroos, despite making more errors than they would have liked. There will be plenty for them to work on before their next hit out.

Great goal kicking from Kelleher tonight – she slots her sixth goal for the match.

It’s been phenomenal defence from Samoa this half, but they give away a penalty and that’s all the invitation the Jillaroos need to find some space and put Sergis through it.

68 mins: Samoa starts with the ball on their own line, but Tagoai drops the ball and Samoa have to defend again. Aiken finds a huge space to run through, but a wall of blue jerseys closes the gap. Penitani-Gray is taken down in a HUGE tackle from Crichton Ropati – it’s the tackle of the match for sure.

66 mins: Samoa’s line drop out doesn’t go the 10m and then they pick it up and are penalised. A huge hit on Kelly when she looks certain to score energises Samoa again – their tryline defence has really been outstanding. Then they hold Johnston up and we take a break while the bunker checks if she’s really held up over the line. Turns out she is! They defend again and stop Australia scoring yet again when they look certain to dive over through Penitani-Gray.

64 mins: Australia get a penalty after a dangerous tackle from Taito and look to add some more points late in the game. Aiken puts in a kick and Upton chase it, but Samoa are there in numbers to kick it dead.

62 mins: The bunker finds that Clarke lost the ball before the line and Australia are on the march down the field again in an instant. A brilliant catch under pressure from Mino-Sinapati and a linebreak from Crichton Ropati gets the ball back down the other end of the field, but Upton picks up the ball from the kick to stop Samoa scoring.

60 mins: Another set for Samoa close to their line – is this their chance to score? They’re getting close, it looks like Clarke dives over, but referee Kasey Badger says she’s short of the line. Samoa decide to challenge the decision.

58 mins: The Jillaroos start to build some momentum again, but a forward pass out on the edge gives the ball back to Samoa – Aiken got a bit overexcited when she saw how big an overlap they had.

56 mins: Samoa are showing so much determination and are working so hard to make something happen. They get a good kick away on the fifth in this set and force Chapman to play at it, earning a line drop out and a repeat set. Nuuasala starts the set strongly with a great run, but they get too close to the sideline on the next tackle and are taken into touch.

54 mins: It’s the first time Samoa have had the ball in good attacking position for a long time and they go close, but they can’t find a strong fifth tackle option – they try to run through a very small gap and have to hand the ball back over to Australia. They defend well again all through the set and force an error late to get a scrum feed just inside their own half.

52 mins: The Jillaroos keep finding themselves deep down in Samoa’s half and they’re testing every bit of the tryline defence. But Samoa hold strong and make try-saving tackle after try-saving tackle. They get a penalty that rewards their great defence and gives them an opportunity in attack.

50 mins: Huge defence from Samoa on their tryline – Kernick wants to push over the line, but they hold her back. She tries an offload, but Isa’ako picks it up for Samoa and powers downfield. A little pause as Masaga gets some medical attention after a big tackle, but she’s OK to continue. A big counterattack from Upton and Chapman when Australia get the ball.

48 mins: A strong set for the Jillaroos following the try and it’s finished with a classic Kelleher fifth tackle kick – an incredibly accurate bomb that is fumbled by Crichton Ropati and Australia have the ball close to the line yet again.

Another easy shot for Kelleher – she’ll be upset her Roosters teammates couldn’t score this close to the post for her during the grand final!

Two tackles after Taufa nearly goes over, Joseph finds some space and dives through a gap to score her first try for the match.

45 mins: Aiken puts a grubber in at the end of Australia’s set and Mino-Sinapati bravely dives on it with chaser coming through. But a couple of tackles later, Hall loses the ball in the tackle and the Jillaroos get a scrum 40m out. One tackle later, they’re on the 10m line and Taufa goes within a whisker of scoring.

43 mins: Some energy in this set from Samoa and a great line break from Rimoni sets them up for a good play, but they can’t get a good kick away on the fifth tackle and the Jillaroos get the ball back.

41 mins: A chance for Samoa in attack and they will want to make some good ground here. Hall pushes up the field well, but the kick is accidentally charged down by Joseph and the Jillaroos are back in great field position. But a forward pass from Upton to Kelly close to the line gives the ball back to Samoa.

39 mins: Fast hands from the Jillaroos off the scrum and they get the ball moving down the field. Aiken throws a great cut out pass, but Chapman can’t hold on to it and Samoa breathe a sigh of relief, as that would have been a certain try.

37 mins: Samoa give away a penalty straight away in the second half for ruck interference – not the start they wanted. But Joseph knocks the ball on early in the set after some strong Samoan defence and they get a scrum in the middle of the field, then throw a forward pass. It’s all happening!

A dominant half from the Jillaroos after they struggled with errors and penalties early. Samoa weren’t able to capitalise with points on the board when they had all the ball and territory – they will be disappointed about that, but they should be proud of the effort.

The professionalism and combinations of the Jillaroos are holding them in good stead at the moment, they were able to build throughout the half and not be thrown off course by things not going to plan early in the half.

Still plenty of excitement yet to come in the second half – take a break and we’ll get back into it soon!

Another easy shot for Kelleher and she knocks it over on the stroke of half time.

Off the back of the penalty, the Jillaroos get one more try before the break, with some quick passing and footwork to put Kernick over.

34 mins: Samoa look to be on struggle street late in the half – they’re not making mistakes, but they don’t look to have the same attacking power they had earlier in the game. But it’s a good sign that they’re still completing their sets. The Jillaroos get a penalty with a minute left in the first half to have one final chance to score in this half.

33 mins: Another opportunity in attack for Samoa after a poor fifth tackle option from Australia, just running out of time to set something up. Masaga makes a great run down the sideline and there’s a good kick at the end of the set, but Upton soars above the crowd to take it safely.

31 mins: A good run from Rimoni caps off a nice set from Samoa, but they can’t put up a good enough kick to deceive the Australians. The Jillaroos dash down field courtesy of a few great line breaks.

29 mins: Johnston starts the set with another strong run, she’s really taking on that ‘post-contact metres’ stat. Kelleher puts up a huge bomb and there’s competition for it, but Mino-Sinapati picks it up and makes a good run.

Kelleher makes no mistake from right in front and adds another two points.

The Jillaroos are really starting to dominate now, after those early mistakes and penalties. It’s not just evident on the scoreboard – where previously the players looked well-matched on the field, now the Jillaroos look stronger and faster. One of the markers loses their footing and Nizza, darts through the space and takes her opportunity to score under the posts.

25 mins: Kelleher misses the conversion and Australia make no mistake in receiving the kick off this time. Johnston makes two great runs up through the middle to put some good metres on. It’s another solid set, pinning Samoa down deep in their own half.

The Jillaroos will take a lot out of that game as well – while they’ll be heartened by the strong win, they will want to cut down their error rate, especially when they come up against New Zealand and England. They made 10 errors and conceded five penalties – many of them at crucial times. I wouldn’t be surprised to see coach Jess Skinner look to mix up some combinations and see if that reduces the error rate.

However, they will be pleased with their 519 post-contact metres and nine line breaks – they are always making things happen out on the field and when they can hold on to the ball they will have the chance to score even more tries.
Both teams have a week off now – Samoa will come up against Wales next Friday back at CommBank Stadium, while the Jillaroos take on England in Perth next Saturday.
I hope you enjoyed this great battle tonight and keep on watching the incredible women playing in all the teams at this tournament. Until next time, go rugby league!

articles.title: Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
articles.summary: Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect to be "on the menu" in the chancellor's Budget tax later this month.
articles.content:
Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC.

Healey has described banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, but leaders in the sector have said it will be "on the menu" at the Budget in two weeks' time.

The biggest four banks collectively made about £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, and trade unions have called for them to face additional taxes.

The trade body for the banking sector, UK Finance, warned "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".

Shares in banks including Lloyds and NatWest fell on Friday on expectations that the sector would be hit by tax hikes. The firms were among the biggest fallers on the UK stock market, with both dropping more than 2%.

Barclays fell only slightly and HSBC actually rose as both have large international businesses and would be less affected by a hike in UK taxes.

There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.

One option is for Healey is to reverse a reduction in the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax, from 8% to 3%, introduced in 2023, by Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt.

Critics argue this would be unfair noting the cut coincided with a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%.

Healey could also raise the bank levy - a small percentage charged on loans.

The BBC understands that the Treasury is leaning towards changing the surcharge if they were to go ahead as it is easier to change an existing tax rather than impose a new windfall tax.

Reversing the 2023 surcharge rate would raise around £2bn. However, the last government was persuaded that adding 8% on top of corporation tax of 25% would leave UK banks struggling to compete with European and US rivals - so it may be that it is raised, but not all the way back to the 8% level.

Speaking to the press in Bangkok, Healey praised the role banks play in the British economy.

Adding that he has "decisions to take in the Budget", he said: "My observation on the banks is that people too often see ​them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future ⁠prospects."

In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.

Sir Philip Augar, an author and former banker in the City of London, told the BBC's Today programme there was "room for a moderate increase" in taxes on the sector that could raise up to £3bn a year.

He said lenders were enjoying "booming conditions", benefiting from higher interest rates which boost their profits.

Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which banks lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.

Sir Philip added that when the banking sector "hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out - when it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment".

He said banks cannot simultaneously be "too big to fail and too big to tax".

Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, which represents trade unions, said Britain's four biggest banks are making a billion pounds a week, with bonuses at post-financial crash records. "These are bumper profits - driven by high interest rates and households' mortgage misery," he said.

"But if the chancellor does ask the Banks to pay a fairer share of tax in the Budget, that's 100% the right call," he added.

Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers onto housing ladder

Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget

Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget

Banks were pleased to have avoided being targeted at the last Budget, given the large profits they have made in recent years.

There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.

Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.

It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.

However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.

A Treasury spokesperson said: "As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals."

Sir Philip Augar, an author and former banker in the City of London, told the BBC's Today programme there was "room for a moderate increase" in taxes on the sector that could raise up to £3bn a year.
He said lenders were enjoying "booming conditions", benefiting from higher interest rates which boost their profits.
Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which banks lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.
Sir Philip added that when the banking sector "hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out - when it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment".
He said banks cannot simultaneously be "too big to fail and too big to tax".

Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, which represents trade unions, said Britain's four biggest banks are making a billion pounds a week, with bonuses at post-financial crash records. "These are bumper profits - driven by high interest rates and households' mortgage misery," he said.
"But if the chancellor does ask the Banks to pay a fairer share of tax in the Budget, that's 100% the right call," he added.
Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers onto housing ladder
Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget
Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget
Banks were pleased to have avoided being targeted at the last Budget, given the large profits they have made in recent years.

There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.

Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.

It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.
However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.

A Treasury spokesperson said: "As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals."

articles.title: What is behind the success of dark skies festival?
articles.summary: Stargazers are preparing to enjoy an annual festival that celebrates the beauty of the night sky.
articles.content:
The Exmoor Dark Skies festival celebrates its 10th anniversary in 2026

Stargazers and astronomers are preparing to enjoy a festival that celebrates the beauty of the night sky.

The annual Exmoor Dark Skies Festival is being held from 16 October to 1 November and this year is its 10th anniversary.

Taking in villages and towns surrounding Exmoor National Park, the event offers walks, talks and shows - putting the dark, clear, night sky into full focus.

But what is the event all about - and what is behind its success over the past decade?

The event celebrates the national park's status as a Dark Sky Reserve.

Granted by the International Astronomical Union in 2011, the status aims to safeguard the right of any citizen to enjoy the night sky by helping to limit light pollution.

Festival organiser Julie Colman said: "We bring together lots and lots of events across the two-week period, celebrating the skies, the wildlife, the wellbeing elements of it."

There are about 80 events taking place across the park, from moonlit swimming and astronomy sessions, to bioluminescence walks and planetarium shows.

Photographers and astronomers can enjoy clear views of the stars during the festival

Colman said there is "very little light pollution on Exmoor", adding it "enables the dark to be really dark with none of the pollution impacting".

"In the core of the reserve, there's an area where there is no light at all in a huge area - and that just makes the sky so much clearer and you're able to see some incredible constellations.

Photographs taken during previous dark skies events show incredibly clear views of the stars against a clear, dark backdrop.

The National Park said it designed the event in 2017 to, in part, help local businesses towards the end of the traditional tourism season.

In Dunster, on the edge of Exmoor, the Yarn Market Hotel manager Antony Brunt said in recent years, "it has become much more widely known - and now we literally have people ringing us up to book".

The hotel hosts special trips during the festival, led by a local astronomer, and runs visits to various sites and events across the park.

Brunt said the festival brings in people from all over the UK, adding: "It's getting to a quieter time of year and these people, they really enjoy coming down.

"We have a group that come each year, in fact, twice a year. For people to come regularly twice a year to the same hotel, they must be enjoying the stargazing part of the weekend."

The growing popularity of the festival meant that many events sold out before the opening day.

articles.title: Álvaro Arbeloa’s push to make Fulham free-flowing is floundering already
articles.summary: Spanish head coach will be under huge pressure if he comes unstuck again at home to Hull on Saturday Fulham fans fretting about life under Álvaro Arbeloa will not feel any better when they remember how things were under Marco Silva, who was one of the most effective managers in the Premier League when it came to making substitutions. Silva’s substitutes were involved in the fourth-highest goal contributions last season and the most in the 2024-25 season. Fulham knew how to dig in and salvage unlikely points. But Silva left last summer, joining Benfica after concluding he could achieve nothing more at Craven Cottage, and his replacement is already under pressure after some puzzling tactical choices. articles.content:
Spanish head coach will be under huge pressure if he comes unstuck again at home to Hull on Saturday

F ulham fans fretting about life under Álvaro Arbeloa will not feel any better when they remember how things were under Marco Silva, who was one of the most effective managers in the Premier League when it came to making substitutions.

Silva’s substitutes were involved in the fourth-highest goal contributions last season and the most in the 2024-25 season. Fulham knew how to dig in and salvage unlikely points. But Silva left last summer, joining Benfica after concluding he could achieve nothing more at Craven Cottage, and his replacement is already under pressure after some puzzling tactical choices.

The worrying shift under Arbeloa was evident during Fulham’s collapse against Ipswich last weekend. The west Londoners were 1-0 up and looking good for their first league win of the season when Arbeloa weakened his midfield by replacing Shea Charles with Manuel Ángel in the 70th minute.

It was a strange way to shut up shop. Charles is physically imposing, has impressed since joining from Southampton and was doing well alongside Sander Berge. The 22-year-old Ángel is 5ft 7in, was making his Premier League debut and has little experience of senior football. Ipswich’s comeback to win 2-1 was not a surprise, particularly when Arbeloa’s other rejigs included bringing on Rodrigo Muniz and switching from a 4-2-3-1 system to a flat 4-4-2 in an attempt to defend the lead.

The subsequent floundering felt inevitable. Emile Smith Rowe, another late substitute, was slow to close down Abdoul Ouattara when the Ipswich right-back equalised. Fulham have dropped eight points from winning positions. They are managing games badly and their physical shortcomings were exposed by Ipswich, whose winner came from a poorly defended free-kick and left Fulham in last place before facing Hull City at home this afternoon.

Arbeloa needs a win. Relegation fears are growing and there are whispers that the Spaniard’s job is under threat. Fulham had a tricky start – they have already faced Chelsea, Liverpool and Manchester United – but the Ipswich game was supposed to mark a turning point. It was the first of three consecutive meetings with the promoted sides and, with Coventry, Hull and Ipswich surpassing expectations, it is easy to see Fulham’s aim to move to a more expansive style under Arbeloa backfiring.

Questions have to be asked over the decision by the Khan family to appoint someone whose experience of management was limited to an interim spell in charge of Real Madrid last season. Fingers will be pointed at the succession planners. Tony Khan, director of football and son of patriarch Shahid, has faced fierce criticism in the past. Silva offered stability. There was always a fear the project would fall apart once the Portuguese was gone.

It does not help Arbeloa to lean on his time at the Bernabéu. He responded to a question about pressure after losing to Ipswich by saying: “I played for the best team in the world … I have coached the best team in the world.” But the optics are awkward. Arbeloa did not win anything as Madrid’s manager, his comments risk making it seem his current employers should be grateful to have him and eyebrows have been raised at three of the 43-year-old’s summer signings coming from his former club.

Ángel, César Palacios and Gonzalo García were all promising young Real Madrid players, all share representation with Arbeloa and are now adapting to a new league. Palacios, an inventive passing midfielder, is 21 and García, a nimble forward, is 22. They deserve to be given time, although the clock is ticking. García, signed for £40m, has one league goal from 18 shots and struggled against Ipswich, winning few duels and pressing ineffectively. Supporters are growing restless. They wonder why Kevin, the Brazilian winger, is being used on the right rather than the left. They feel Arbeloa is chopping and changing too often. They worry about the team conceding costly late goals against Sunderland, Crystal Palace and United. Fulham were ridiculously open in their opening game, the barmy 3-2 defeat by Chelsea , and their expected goals against is 10.3 in six games. They have lost two of their main goalscorers, Raúl Jiménez and Harry Wilson, and are struggling to fill the void.

Equally there is an argument that Arbeloa needs time to implement a new style. There are suggestions some players are unsure about the manager’s tactics. Some stalwarts have been sidelined – Joachim Andersen, the influential Denmark centre-back, is not suited to playing a high line and has lost his spot to David Affengruber – but perhaps a refresh was required. Fulham have looked to lower the age of their squad, in part because of a need to comply with financial regulations, and there is nothing intrinsically wrong with trying to play more exciting football.

There have been encouraging spells. After flirting with European qualification in each of the past four seasons, only to fizzle out and finish in the bottom half, Fulham can be forgiven for wondering how to take the next step. At the same time the fear for supporters is that a club operating with one of the league’s smaller budgets have forgotten what it takes to survive. Silva’s teams could attack but were gritty and streetwise. At the moment Arbeloa looks naive. Fulham lost £45m in the last financial year and spent a lot on the Riverside Stand refurbishment. The Khans need Premier League survival. Arbeloa has big ideas but might not make it past this month without a huge improvement.

articles.title: The WSL so far: goal-shy Arsenal, underrated Brighton and more data pointers
articles.summary: The Gunners’ title hopes look over after five games as draws continue from last season while the Seagulls, actually ninth, are third for expected points The Women’s Super League table is taking shape for 2026-27. The defending champions, Manchester City, have five wins from five games but more intriguing stories lie elsewhere. Why are Arsenal struggling, who is performing better than results suggest, and in which way are two promoted teams smashing expectations? Here are three key data points. Continue reading...
articles.content:
The Gunners’ title hopes look over after five games as draws continue from last season while the Seagulls, actually ninth, are third for expected points

T he Women’s Super League table is taking shape for 2026-27. The defending champions, Manchester City, have five wins from five games but more intriguing stories lie elsewhere. Why are Arsenal struggling, who is performing better than results suggest, and in which way are two promoted teams smashing expectations? Here are three key data points.

Opta made Arsenal third favourites to win the WSL before a ball was kicked. Their win at Brighton combined with Chelsea’s draw against Aston Villa in week one meant Renée Slegers’ side rose to narrow favourites. The four games since, from which Arsenal took two points, have torpedoed their title chances.

One reason for their slump is a continuation of a problem from last season. The stats section of our Arsenal pre-season preview highlighted draws in 2025-26 that they deserved to win based on expected goals. That trend has continued this season with positive xG margins of 2.2 and 1.2 in their home games against Crystal Palace (0-0) and Manchester United (1-1) respectively.

Had Smilla Holmberg not scored with her only shot of the campaign in the 95th minute against United, the situation would be even worse. While players inevitably have a small sample of shots at this point, Arsenal’s finishing woes are a collective problem. Only Lisa Baum and Alessia Russo have also scored, with the latter 1.28 goals below her expected goal tally. Scoring three goals in the international break may help Russo’s confidence.

A physical deficiency may also be contributing to Arsenal’s struggles. Gradient Sports award players an athleticism score, a single metric which incorporates stamina, explosiveness and game context. There are 125 WSL players with a score who have played at least 270 minutes this season. Steph Catley is Arsenal’s highest-ranked player, at 31st, and their only representative above 59th. Every other club has at least two players in the top 50, with Chelsea having five. West Ham possessing seven shows this is not a decisive factor in success but Arsenal fans may wonder whether their side need to increase the physical intensity.

Brighton were predicted by Opta to finish seventh. As they are ninth, that forecast looks reasonable enough. Yet the underlying data suggests they deserve to be third, 0.1 expected points behind City. The Seagulls endured a case of wastefulness more extreme than anything Arsenal have offered up when they drew 1-1 with Villa. Despite an expected goal count of 3.17 to 0.03 in Brighton’s favour, Lynn Wilms’s 89th-minute goal robbed them of a victory.

Brighton also drew at Birmingham when leading the expected goals by 1.5 and missed four Opta-defined big chances in their 2-0 defeat at London City Lionesses . If they can make their dominance count, Brighton look capable of at least matching the fifth-place finish they secured in 2024-25.

Productive pressing tends to belong to better teams. Opta’s high turnover metric records when a team win the ball to begin a new sequence of open-play possession within 40m of the opposition goal. If you sort the 2025-26 WSL by the number of high turnovers that led to shots, the five clubs with the fewest were those that finished in the bottom five. The standings were slightly more jumbled if you looked at the percentage of high turnovers that generated shots, to assess effectiveness and efficiency, but the top four teams for this finished in the WSL top five. Promoted London City had the fourth-least productive press by this measure.

Two of their successors are upending these correlations. Palace are third for shot-ending high turnovers, with 12, behind Chelsea (17) and Tottenham (15). The percentage of their possession regains in the final 40m that led to shots is the highest in the division (33.3%), with their fellow promoted side Birmingham (28.6%) next in line.

The West Midlands club are tied with Tottenham for most goals from high turnovers, on three (while Palace have two). Birmingham’s goals were all scored by Océane Hurtré, helping propel her to joint-first in the golden boot race, with five goals.

The 22-year-old French attacker won the ball for two of the three high-turnover goals, including one at Manchester City. Hurtré’s others came in the first and eighth minutes of matches against Palace and Brighton respectively, illustrating the benefit that pressing opponents early can bring.

articles.title: From the Octagon to Quantico: UFC teaching the FBI to fight is its latest tie to Trump world

articles.content:
The mixed martial arts organization has had links to the US president for years. Now it could be involved in training federal agents

I n the lead-up to UFC Freedom 250 – the cagefighting spectacle that took place on the South Lawn of the White House to mark Donald Trump’s 80th birthday this past summer – the FBI announced that a handful of UFC fighters would visit the bureau for an exclusive training seminar for federal agents.

Taking place at the FBI Special Agent Academy in Quantico, Virginia, the March seminar put roughly 300 federal agents and academy students through specialized hand-to-hand combat training with seven past and current UFC fighters, including former middleweight champion Chris Weidman, who was pictured giving attendees advice on warding off attackers.

The two-day seminar included photo-ops with the fighters, who wore branded UFC-FBI training gear. FBI director Kash Patel also posed for photos with federal agents, and appeared to be handing out signed headshots of himself.

“[UFC CEO] Dana White has changed the game in the mixed martial arts industry and we’re extremely honored to be partnered with him, the professionals, and the UFC,” Patel said in the UFC press release . “We are grateful for their shared love of our nation, so that we can better defend her.”

Now, six months after the initial seminar, the FBI appears to be in the process of awarding the UFC an exclusive contract to train agents in mixed martial arts, further cementing the relationship between the fighting organization and the Trump administration .

In September, the bureau filed a Sole Source Justification form, a document that allows the government to award contracts without considering bids from other companies. The bureau claimed that the UFC was “uniquely qualified” to provide these services, noting in the form that “the trainers provided by UFC have the skills necessary to instruct striking techniques, grappling/takedowns, weapon defense, ground control, as well as conditioning to the standard that the FBI expects and requires.”

The document says that the exclusive contract would be limited to a single year, while a potential long-term contract would be open to competitive bidding following “market research.” The exact sum that the FBI plans to pay the UFC is not disclosed.

The FBI claims the UFC collaboration is part of an initiative to provide innovative training for its agents, but it also appears to be a part of the sustained consolidation of the UFC-Trump alliance.

Over the past decade, the UFC has emerged as one of Trump’s most influential and reliable partners. The promotion’s owner, Ari Emanuel, was once Trump’s agent and has helped steer the UFC’s rightward shift. White is a close friend of the president , and has stumped for him over the course of three presidential campaigns. White also claimed responsibility for Trump’s media strategy to bypass traditional media in favor of alternative platforms within the “manosphere” catering to young men – a course of action that helped him secure reelection in November 2024.

The UFC has also gone to great lengths to platform Trump and his political agenda. The organization produced a propaganda documentary on Trump called Combatant-in-Chief , which perpetuated the lie that Trump was instrumental to the UFC’s survival during a dark period in its history. Trump welcomed the attention, basking in the admiration of the UFC’s conservative-leaning male audience. He cultivated relationships with fighters, leveraging their support to portray himself as a symbolic strongman. He has embraced the UFC’s culture of defiance, machismo and spectacle to help buttress his image as a rebel against liberal norms.

Since then, the UFC has been rewarded handsomely for its loyalty, not least by becoming the first professional sports brand to host an event at the White House – a propaganda spectacle that blended patriotism with bloodlust for a night of authoritarian theatre .

The Trump administration has also formalized its relationship with the UFC by signing a memorandum of understanding with the US Department of State to begin “sports diplomacy” initiatives, further integrating the promotion into official government policy and soft power strategy. The UFC also began a sponsorship deal with Anduril, a controversial defense tech start-up known for developing AI-powered war machines and sentry towers used to survey the US-Mexico border. Anduril happens to be a key beneficiary of the Trump administration’s ongoing effort to reindustrialize the US military.

The UFC continues to benefit from its allegiance to Trump, most recently through the FBI training program.

The UFC-FBI program is far from unique: military and police forces around the world have undergone unarmed combat training. In 2024, the Canadian military organized jiu-jitsu seminars for various units. Gulf states such as the UAE incorporate Brazilian jiu-jitsu practice in their military and police training. Several FBI agents also have experience with unarmed combat, including retired agent George Piro, who led the FBI’s interrogation of Saddam Hussein. After retiring from the bureau, Piro won his division at the IBJJF (International Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu Federation) World No-Gi Championship.

But, even given that history, the FBI’s UFC partnership reeks of favoritism. While it remains unclear how the training program will be structured or which fighters will be selected to lead the seminars, it is worth noting that several of the UFC fighters who took part in the training seminar in March 2026 were affiliated with the Trump administration, or with Patel personally. For example, former UFC fighter Jorge Masvidal headlined a “Fighters Against Socialism” tour across Florida alongside Donald Trump Jr ahead of the 2020 election. Another trainer at the March seminar, UFC lightweight champion Justin Gaethje, stumped for Trump on numerous occasions, including at the 2026 midterm convention in Dallas , where he urged Republicans to vote with the same gusto they did in 2024.

Several of the fighters at the training seminar were also managed by Ali Abdelaziz, a controversial figure in the sport who once worked as an informant for the FBI and the New York Police Department . He was recruited to work undercover collecting intelligence on a terrorism-linked organization named Muslims of the Americas but his covert relationship with the US government was eventually severed when agents reportedly had suspicions about his reliability .

Despite his controversial past, Abdelaziz emerged as one of the most influential managers in mixed martial arts, with a roster of clients packed with past and current UFC champions. He also established relationships with Maga operatives like Richard Grenell, who served as acting director of national intelligence under Trump in 2020, as well as with Patel. Abdelaziz used his position as a manager and public figure to campaign for Patel to land the FBI director role, even utilizing his roster of fighters’ social media accounts to spread the word. He later attended Patel’s Senate confirmation hearing and was present at the joint UFC-FBI training seminar. Last month, Abdelaziz was pictured partying with the FBI director at the wedding for Trump’s former lawyer Alina Habba – despite once being suspected of being a double agent by the same federal agency that Patel now runs.

While Patel may continue to make a case for a partnership with the UFC, the truth is that this is merely the latest example of how MMA – and the UFC in particular – have become deeply intertwined with US politics , especially among Republicans eager to bask in the reflected glory of the literal tough guys they’re bringing into the fold.

articles.title: Infantino told by top Fifa figures to scrap or depoliticise peace prize after Trump furore
articles.summary: Backlash greeted award of prize to US president Fifa committee to make recommendations this year Donald Trump is likely to end up as the only political leader awarded the Fifa peace prize after Gianni Infantino was told at Thursday’s meeting of the Fifa council to make major changes or scrap the controversial award. The Guardian has learned that several council members demanded the award be abolished and others called for the prize to be depoliticised, with Fifa’s football social responsibility committee to make a recommendation before the next council meeting in Doha on 16 December. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Donald Trump is likely to end up as the only political leader awarded the Fifa peace prize after Gianni Infantino was told at Thursday’s meeting of the Fifa council to make major changes or scrap the controversial award.

The Guardian has learned that several council members demanded the award be abolished and others called for the prize to be depoliticised, with Fifa’s football social responsibility committee to make a recommendation before the next council meeting in Doha on 16 December.

Infantino announced the peace prize had been handed to the social responsibility committee at the start of Thursday’s meeting. Council members returned to the subject later in a series of questions about possible conflict of interests at Fifa.

There is a strong view among council members that the peace prize in its current form is tainted by association with Trump, with some raising concerns that the US president could object and create a diplomatic storm if he does not like the identity of its next recipient.

Fifa’s 22-person social responsibility committee is dominated by representatives from countries loyal to Infantino so abolition may be avoided on the grounds it would represent a humiliation for the Fifa president, although there is a widespread acceptance that change is required.

One council member told the Guardian the most likely outcome discussed is the reinvention of the peace prize as an award for an individual within football who has delivered exceptional work promoting social harmony and responsibility, with a provision stating it cannot be given to a politician.

Article two of Fifa’s statutes prohibits any political or governmental interference in football, one of several reasons why honouring Trump last year triggered such a backlash from many members.

Fifa announced the creation of its peace prize last November with a stipulation that it would “reward individuals who have taken exceptional and extraordinary actions for peace and by doing so have united people across the world”.

Trump was given the award at the men’s World Cup draw in Washington last December, with Infantino presenting the US president with a golden trophy, a medal and a certificate, but the process behind his selection has never been made public.

The social responsibility committee is expected as part of its review to set strict parameters for any surviving award, and to provide details of a nomination and selection procedure.

articles.title: Do Premier League teams really need to run more to win matches?
articles.summary: Pundits regularly criticise teams for not running enough but is there a link between distance covered and results? By Opta Analyst It was like clockwork. Manchester United dropped points against Tottenham and critics were quick to question their effort and application, using the team’s physical statistics to make points. Speaking on Sky Sports, Jamie Redknapp said: “There’s a pattern I don’t really like when I watch teams, and that’s when – and the stats don’t lie – the other team runs more than you. In the Premier League right now, I feel there are a couple of non-negotiables: you’ve got to run more than the other team if you want to win, or at least get close enough that it doesn’t make that much of a difference. Tottenham ran five kilometres more than Manchester United.” Continue reading...
articles.content:
Pundits regularly criticise teams for not running enough but is there a link between distance covered and results?

It was like clockwork. Manchester United dropped points against Tottenham and critics were quick to question their effort and application, using the team’s physical statistics to make points.

Speaking on Sky Sports, Jamie Redknapp said: “There’s a pattern I don’t really like when I watch teams, and that’s when – and the stats don’t lie – the other team runs more than you. In the Premier League right now, I feel there are a couple of non-negotiables: you’ve got to run more than the other team if you want to win, or at least get close enough that it doesn’t make that much of a difference. Tottenham ran five kilometres more than Manchester United.”

Physical metrics such as distance run and number of sprints are increasingly accessible and easy to understand, so have fallen into common use. It’s become a common theme that, when a big club fail to meet expectations, pundits and commentators look to their running metrics in search of one catch-all explanation. Liverpool and Chelsea were the targets of similar judgment last season.

But is it fair? How much of a correlation is there between a team running lots and that team being successful? While the numbers may not be complex at face value, answering this question is, which probably highlights that such metrics are so nuanced in a team sport that it probably isn’t best practice to tie too much significance to the topline figures.

The first way we can assess it is by comparing the Premier League table to the rankings of distance run and high-intensity distance. Yes, this is pretty simple and rudimentary, but it’s a place to start.

Last season’s Premier League table hardly mirrors the rankings for distance covered or high-intensity distance per game. Sure, Arsenal and Manchester City were high for overall distance, but the teams who came third to eighth had middling – at best – outputs in this respect.

The teams that finished in the top 10 averaged 4,363km over the season; the teams in the bottom 10 averaged 4,332km. In the grand scheme of things, a difference of 31km between those averages is rather small.

Again, there’s a slight difference between the average high-intensity distance for top-10 teams (338.7km) and those in the bottom 10 (328.4km), but we’re talking about an increase of 3%. Similarly when perusing data from this season, it’s difficult to see much of a link.

Looking at it in relation to the table does ignore that success is relative, however. Of course Burnley were not going to finish seventh in the table just because they came seventh in the distance rankings.

Instead, we can use the Opta supercomputer’s pre-season predictions to give us an idea of what a successful campaign might have looked like for all clubs and whether there was a trend of overachieving teams running more.

Ten teams in the Premier League last season finished at least one place higher than their likeliest final place according to the Opta supercomputer in pre-season, and they averaged 4,369km over the season; the nine clubs that finished at least a place below their likeliest final position averaged 4,308km. So again, there is a difference, it’s just very small at 1.4%.

However, Sunderland (+13 places) and Manchester United (+9 places) weren’t in the top 10 for distance covered but exceeded the supercomputer’s expectations to a greater degree than any other team; Crystal Palace (-8 places) and Newcastle (-6 places) were in the top 10 for ground covered but among the most disappointing teams relative to pre-season expectations.

We can also look at expected points, a model that simulates the goals scored by each side in each match based on the xG value of all shots and then simulates every game 10,000 times to determine the proportion that the fixtures end with a win, draw or defeat. It isn’t perfect because it’s limited by the natural pitfalls of xG, but it does give a decent barometer of performance over a season.

The teams that ranked in the bottom half for distance covered last term exceeded their xPts totals by 0.38 on average, whereas the teams that ranked in the top half for that metric claimed 1.88 points fewer than their xPts on average. In short, then, it would appear there’s very little correlation between success (at least in the ways we’ve tried to depict it) over a long period and running distance.

But that doesn’t mean we didn’t find any correlation across the board. When analysing a host of physical metrics over the course of 2025-26, the one that showed the strongest link to the final standings was distance covered in possession .

It isn’t perfect but there is the hint of a correlation between more distance run on the ball and finishing higher up the table. That doesn’t necessarily mean a certain team finished high because they ran more in possession; it’s likely a reflection of that side having more of the ball owing to possessing better players. It still felt notable, though.

But perhaps the greatest link between physical metrics and success would appear to come on a game level, rather than over a full season. Since the start of last season, there have been 86 instances in the Premier League of a team covering at least 5km less than their opponents in a game. In those 86 matches, the side that covered at least 5km less have won 10 times, and seven of those were expected victories according to the Opta supercomputer. That’s a win rate of 11.6%.

Now, there are some obvious caveats here. Most importantly, 20 of these games involved at least one of the teams having a player sent off, and that can obviously have a big impact on both teams’ physical output.

Excluding those 20 games, we are left with eight wins for the team that covered at least 5km less than their opponents from 66 matches; that means the win rate shoots up from 11.6% to a massive … 12.1%.

When we change the parameters to look at instances when one team covered between 2.5km and 4.99km less than their opponents (but excluding games with a red card), the win rate does improve to 25.8%, though that’s still not especially high. The loss rate is 46%.

This suggests, then, some relationship between the most extreme examples of outrunning the opposition and winning. But we shouldn’t jump to conclusions; we can’t be absolutely sure the additional running is any more decisive than a whole range of other factors.

Physical metrics are also often closely tied to playing style, so one team’s output in a match can directly affect that of their opposition. The reason many like to lean on these figures is probably because, on the face of it, they are so simple to understand and very easy – rightly or wrongly – to attribute to effort, especially if you’re talking about a team that have lost.

But the fact there’s no strong correlation between distance run over a full season and success arguably suggests the answer over the long term isn’t to run your team into the ground, instead knowing when to up the intensity for maximum effect.

Jürgen Klopp perhaps summed it up best right at the start of his Liverpool reign. “We don’t have to run 115km per match to be successful. You don’t have to run like crazy if you have the ball. It is only the start. We must know how to turn the screws in the right moment; better thinking, better timing. But if we play a much better team and you are not ready to run more than them, then you are crazy.”

Pep Guardiola added to that in his final season at Manchester City. “It’s about when you have to run. Running just to run? I can go to the track and ask the marathon guys to play for us. It’s not about that, it’s when you have to do it. Last season when some players ran it was useless. The most important thing is the combination of both things.”

Intent and timing. When the going gets tough, intent potentially overrides all else in the eyes of the average fan. To be seen to be lacking effort, whether that reflects reality or not, is a cardinal sin in a struggling football team. But rarely is “just run more” the answer.

Looking at it in relation to the table does ignore that success is relative, however. Of course Burnley were not going to finish seventh in the table just because they came seventh in the distance rankings.

Instead, we can use the Opta supercomputer’s pre-season predictions to give us an idea of what a successful campaign might have looked like for all clubs and whether there was a trend of overachieving teams running more.

Ten teams in the Premier League last season finished at least one place higher than their likeliest final place according to the Opta supercomputer in pre-season, and they averaged 4,369km over the season; the nine clubs that finished at least a place below their likeliest final position averaged 4,308km. So again, there is a difference, it’s just very small at 1.4%.

However, Sunderland (+13 places) and Manchester United (+9 places) weren’t in the top 10 for distance covered but exceeded the supercomputer’s expectations to a greater degree than any other team; Crystal Palace (-8 places) and Newcastle (-6 places) were in the top 10 for ground covered but among the most disappointing teams relative to pre-season expectations.

We can also look at expected points, a model that simulates the goals scored by each side in each match based on the xG value of all shots and then simulates every game 10,000 times to determine the proportion that the fixtures end with a win, draw or defeat. It isn’t perfect because it’s limited by the natural pitfalls of xG, but it does give a decent barometer of performance over a season.

The teams that ranked in the bottom half for distance covered last term exceeded their xPts totals by 0.38 on average, whereas the teams that ranked in the top half for that metric claimed 1.88 points fewer than their xPts on average. In short, then, it would appear there’s very little correlation between success (at least in the ways we’ve tried to depict it) over a long period and running distance.

But that doesn’t mean we didn’t find any correlation across the board. When analysing a host of physical metrics over the course of 2025-26, the one that showed the strongest link to the final standings was distance covered in possession .

It isn’t perfect but there is the hint of a correlation between more distance run on the ball and finishing higher up the table. That doesn’t necessarily mean a certain team finished high because they ran more in possession; it’s likely a reflection of that side having more of the ball owing to possessing better players. It still felt notable, though.

But perhaps the greatest link between physical metrics and success would appear to come on a game level, rather than over a full season. Since the start of last season, there have been 86 instances in the Premier League of a team covering at least 5km less than their opponents in a game. In those 86 matches, the side that covered at least 5km less have won 10 times, and seven of those were expected victories according to the Opta supercomputer. That’s a win rate of 11.6%.

Now, there are some obvious caveats here. Most importantly, 20 of these games involved at least one of the teams having a player sent off, and that can obviously have a big impact on both teams’ physical output.

Excluding those 20 games, we are left with eight wins for the team that covered at least 5km less than their opponents from 66 matches; that means the win rate shoots up from 11.6% to a massive … 12.1%.

When we change the parameters to look at instances when one team covered between 2.5km and 4.99km less than their opponents (but excluding games with a red card), the win rate does improve to 25.8%, though that’s still not especially high. The loss rate is 46%.

This suggests, then, some relationship between the most extreme examples of outrunning the opposition and winning. But we shouldn’t jump to conclusions; we can’t be absolutely sure the additional running is any more decisive than a whole range of other factors.

Physical metrics are also often closely tied to playing style, so one team’s output in a match can directly affect that of their opposition. The reason many like to lean on these figures is probably because, on the face of it, they are so simple to understand and very easy – rightly or wrongly – to attribute to effort, especially if you’re talking about a team that have lost.

But the fact there’s no strong correlation between distance run over a full season and success arguably suggests the answer over the long term isn’t to run your team into the ground, instead knowing when to up the intensity for maximum effect.

Jürgen Klopp perhaps summed it up best right at the start of his Liverpool reign. “We don’t have to run 115km per match to be successful. You don’t have to run like crazy if you have the ball. It is only the start. We must know how to turn the screws in the right moment; better thinking, better timing. But if we play a much better team and you are not ready to run more than them, then you are crazy.”

Pep Guardiola added to that in his final season at Manchester City. “It’s about when you have to run. Running just to run? I can go to the track and ask the marathon guys to play for us. It’s not about that, it’s when you have to do it. Last season when some players ran it was useless. The most important thing is the combination of both things.”

Intent and timing. When the going gets tough, intent potentially overrides all else in the eyes of the average fan. To be seen to be lacking effort, whether that reflects reality or not, is a cardinal sin in a struggling football team. But rarely is “just run more” the answer.

articles.content:
It’s been 25 years since the release of this film skewering an industry that famously takes itself very seriously. It might have been comedy gold but it was also, in its own way, prophetic

C ritics were divided, the US release date couldn’t have been worse (a few days after 9/11) and the sequel was a flop. Yet few films have predicted fashion’s own present like 2001’s Zoolander. The memeable absurdist comedy about the “three-times male model of the year” was a cinematic Cassandra: correctly predicting themes, styles and sensibilities of the industry that still ring true today.

The joke around Derek Zoolander’s trademark look, the Blue Steel, was how ridiculous it was. Still, the shocked but vacant stare with the exaggerated pout later became the facial pose on social media. Officially defined as “duck face” (after the Japanese term “ahiru-guchi”, duck mouth), the look gained traction on Instagram in the early 2010s, when people finally took a break from smizing. But tweakments such as lip-filler and forehead botox mean that faces have begun artificially morphing into the pose. So now everyone can be really, really, really Zoolander, without even trying.

There is a popular theory that Trump crept into the hearts and minds of the American public through his appearances on his reality TV show The Apprentice. But he also made fleeting cameos in films such as Two Weeks Notice, Little Rascals and Home Alone 2. His one line in Zoolander? “Without Derek Zoolander, male modelling wouldn’t be what it is today.” A fabulous little fib that he imparts very believably. Shocking to hear in 2026, I know.

The morning after the VH1 Fashion Awards, Derek and his model flatmates Brint, Rufus and Meekus (played by Alexander Skarsgård) are all hanging out, when Zoolander’s nightwear of choice is revealed to be a onesie covered in penguins. A decade later the onesie would become ubiquitous, with high-street sales skyrocketing after One Direction brought them into people’s living rooms . File next to man-buns – and never forget Zoolander did them first.

At the start of the film, a shady fashion cartel are intent on keeping sweat shop labour going, despite the prime minister of Malaysia’s plan to ban it. One fiendish fashionista complains: “50% of my inventory is manufactured in sweat shops in Malaysia!” Zoolander satirised fashion’s cognitive dissonance about sweat shop labour deftly. 25 years on, it’s still, tragically, very much an issue .

Donatella Versace likes her espresso served in a pink-and-gold china cup , Anna Wintour’s order is reportedly a grande, extra-hot whole-milk latte from Starbucks , while Calvin Klein infamously got his staff to compare the hue of his milky coffee to a Pantone colour swatch to get it “just right”. In the film, Derek, Meekus, Brint and Rufus share a love of the orange mocha frappuccino, while freaky designer Mugatu (Will Ferrell) loses it when his latte is too foamy. Fashion’s niche drinks orders have arguably only become more extreme – as any fashion intern with a long list of hyper-specific morning matcha and iced coffee orders will tell you.

Zoolander has more guest stars than an episode of Friends. Hi David Bowie, Tommy Hilfiger, Paris Hilton, Gwen Stefani, Tom Ford, Winona Ryder, Mark Ronson, Donatella Versace, Lil Kim and Sandra Bernhard. Groaning under the weight of its own star power, there is one cameo that feels slightly more significant than the others. Victoria Beckham delivers the line “he’s a fashion icon!” about Derek. Given her move from non-smiling Spice Girl to non-smiling creative director in the last 25 years, she could have been talking about herself.

When Derek announces his early retirement from modelling at the triple funeral of his flatmates (“I’m sure there’s a lot more to life than being really, really good looking,”) the assembled mourners are shocked. But the surprise catwalk curtain call has become familiar: Jean Paul Gaultier stood down in 2020 after 50 fantastique years , Dries Van Noten said goodbye in 2024, while stylist Law Roach “retired” on Instagram in 2023 before sneaking back two years later. Cheeky. Even Derek himself came out of retirement for Zoolander 2.

“Not many people read your Time magazine, or whatever it’s called,” Derek tells journalist Matilda. At the time of release this was a joke at the expense of our model hero. Time magazine’s paid circulation was 4m copies per week. Now, not only is Time’s paid digital circulation at about 370,000 but many of the fashion magazines featured in the film have long ceased production: Look, Marie Claire and InStyle to name but a few. Hearing that line in 2026, it hits differently. Earth to Matilda, Derek was right, not many people are reading your magazine (although maybe they are reading your Substack).

Mugatu’s Derelicte collection, crassly inspired by unhoused people, was a stinging comment on how far-removed fashion can be from reality. While John Galliano had already produced a collection inspired by those living along the Seine and purses resembling bin bags did appear on the catwalk (Lanvin) , the Derelicte collection, which included a battered cardboard box worn as a dress, a feather boa of inflated condoms and a cape made of rubbish, picked at a concept which the likes of Demna later focused in on at Vetements and Balenciaga, elevating wear-and-tear as the distressed look.
