articles.content:
The engaging TV doctor dismantles the spurious science behind modern day snake oils, from collagen to turmeric

W hen Xand van Tulleken set off on a journey into the wild west of wellness, he didn’t expect to discover anything new about vitamin D. Of all the supplements that line our shelves and social media feeds, it ought to be the least controversial; even the NHS website, which is hardly a wellspring of quackery, advises that everyone should consider taking a daily dose during autumn and winter, when we risk becoming deficient (D is the vitamin we get mostly from sunlight, and which helps keep our bones strong).

The tiggerish TV doctor and twin brother to Chris (he’s the one who wrote Ultra-Processed People about the food industry) qualified at a time of high excitement in vitamin D circles; in the early 2000s, big studies were linking it not just to bone health but cancer, heart disease and dementia. “The range of potential problems to be solved was dizzying,” Van Tulleken writes in Make Me Well.

But – spoiler alert – it turns out evidence even of the benefits of the most medically endorsed supplement shrivels under scrutiny. After immersing himself in decades of trials and speaking to a professor who had devoted his career to what he now views as the false promise of vitamin D, Van Tulleken finds no justification for its routine consumption for all but a tiny proportion of the population who are genuinely deficient.

The vitamin D chapter follows what becomes a familiar and compelling pattern in Van Tulleken’s first proper solo book, in which he combines the rigour of an investigative journalist with medical expertise and the bouncy bedside manner that makes him such a natural broadcaster. He’s also the best kind of science writer, leaning into complexity while making it as easy to digest as a fish oil gummy (another thing you might want to stop forking out for).

As well as vitamin D, he goes deep on collagen, testosterone, multivitamins, turmeric and krill oil supplements, as well as the burgeoning markets for personalised nutrition, glucose monitoring, wearable tech and private blood screening. In each case, he finds a troubling blurring of the lines between wellness and healthcare – and yawning gaps between hype and the evidence. He also uncovers the harm that wellness fads can do to our bodies, our relationship with food and the environment.

In a chapter devoted to collagen, Van Tulleken travels to China to learn how a messy byproduct of the meat industry has been marketed as a modern elixir with a mark-up of as much as 1,000%. Ejiao, a premium kind of donkey-derived collagen, has become such a coveted source of “ingestible beauty” that manufacturers have exhausted Chinese supplies of donkey hides; soon rural communities in countries across Africa were finding that their animals were being slaughtered for export so that their skins could be boiled up and turned into expensive gummies and powders.

He also explores the history and booming business of supplements, from the literal snake oil of the late 19th century to an unwholesome contemporary market driven by podcasts, influencers and a scientific publishing industry that appears to have striking deficiencies of its own: “The more research I do, the more I see the same patterns repeatedly: conflicts of interest, industry-funded trials, industry-­owned journals and an entire system designed to exploit people.”

“The right people to make you well won’t be health gurus,” Van Tulleken says at the end of a book that deserves to prompt some kind of industry reckoning. “They might be dance instructors or librarians or martial arts teachers or the person who runs your local choir.” While I consider resuming reacquainting myself with my own piano, I have no plans to dust off my bottle of vitamin D pills as the nights draw in.

articles.title: Snapchat and Instagram grooming becoming 'easier'
articles.summary: Online grooming is rising, with children as young as five targeted, prompting calls for reform.
articles.content:
Experts warn children as young as five years old are now being groomed on social media and gaming sites

Experts are urging parents to talk to their children amid warnings social media grooming is becoming "quicker" and "easier" than ever before.

Childline said Snapchat, TikTok and Instagram were the top platforms children named in counselling about online sexual abuse last year. The companies have been approached for comment.

Avon and Somerset Police's child exploitation prevention officer Andri Nicolau said children as young as five can be targeted through social media, gaming and messaging platforms. She urged parents to encourage kids to ask for help without fear of blame or punishment.

The warning comes after three men were jailed for grooming a 17-year-old girl on Snapchat before raping her.

Research by the NSPCC found sexual communication offences involving children in the South West have more than doubled since the offence was introduced seven years ago, to 756 in 2024/25.

Of those, 300 were recorded by Avon and Somerset Police, 96 by Gloucestershire Constabulary and 61 by Wiltshire Police.

The charity also said Snapchat was mentioned in 324 counselling sessions about online sexual abuse between April 2025 and March 2026, a 19% increase on the previous year.

TikTok (234) and Instagram (197) were the next most frequently mentioned platforms.

Chris Sherwood, chief executive of the NSPCC, said: "It's deeply disturbing that hundreds of children have come to us in the past year alone, disclosing experiences of online sexual abuse linked to these popular apps and platforms.

"These crimes are highly distressing for victims, often leaving children and their families to deal with devastating lifelong impacts."

Suleman Aqeel, 23, was charged with 29 sexual and violent offences, including raping and sexually abusing a woman and a child in Bristol

Another recent example involved Suleman Aqeel, from Speedwell in Bristol, who was jailed for 17 years at Bristol Crown Court on 30 September.

Aqeel used social media, including Snapchat, to arrange to meet young girls. He also filmed some of his offences and threatened to share intimate videos and images.

New data suggests that this particular form of exploitation of children, known as 'sextortion', has also reached record levels.

The Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) said there has been a sharp rise in the number of young people contacting its confidential Report Remove helpline , external because they fear sexual images of themselves have been shared, or could be shared, online.

Criminals try to extort or blackmail their victims by threatening to publish the images, which have often been taken by the child themselves.

Nicolau said children spending more time online meant they were increasingly vulnerable to grooming, which is "easier" and "quicker" than ever before.

"With online gaming and social media, you have kids from five years old online, some of them have their own phones, so it can be any age," she said.

She works with schools to inform children how to be safe online, but said they are often unaware of the risks, including not viewing people they meet online as strangers and expecting them to be "nasty" from the start.

Nicolau encouraged any child or young person who believes they are being groomed to "find someone they are comfortable with and speak to them".

She said the police might not be the first choice, but speaking to somebody they trust is what mattered.

Nicolau urged parents to talk to their children and not take away devices or ban them from platforms, warning this could make them feel they were to blame.

"Sit down with your child, tell them it's not their fault, even if they've sent indecent images of themselves," she said.

"Believe them and give them the authorisation to say whatever they need to say."

Andri Nicolau, Avon and Somerset Police's child exploitation prevention officer, works with schools to inform children about the risks of online grooming

Ella Bradshaw, the NSPCC's policy and public affairs officer, advised parents to start conversations about online safety as early as possible so that children know that they have a "safe adult" to go to.

"Often, particularly if it's to do with grooming or any kind of sexual or romantic relationship, children can be really scared of being judged and embarrassed to talk," said Bradshaw.

"Making sure that your child knows that you will stand by them, that you will respond with warmth and care rather than judging them or blaming them for what's going on is really important."

James Simmons-Read, who leads the Children's Society national exploitation prevention programme, said there are "huge concerns" about the growing scale of child sexual abuse and exploitation online.

"Perpetrators are always adapting ways they can better reach young people, whether that's through gaming or social media," he said.

He said another worrying trend was young people turning to AI rather than adults for advice and support about online harms.

Simmons-Read urged parents to normalise conversations with young people about their online lives.

Ella Bradshaw from the NSPCC said children don't speak out because of fear of judgment

Ellen Roome, from Cheltenham, who has been campaigning for improvements to online safety since the death of her son Jools in 2022, said not enough is being done to protect young people on social media.

"Children are regularly being fed content that is either violent or grooming material and I think as it stands, there isn't any platform that is fully safe for them," she said.

"I do think that the social media ban for children will help, but they need to make sure that it is enforced and social media companies are held to account."

Ellen Roome has secured rights for families to get social media data from their children's accounts after they pass away.

Simmons-Read said the social media ban for under 16s , which is due to come into force in 2027, "doesn't go far enough", could be bypassed by criminals and could even discourage young people from speaking up about online grooming.

"We want tech platforms to invest more in detecting exploitation when it's happening on their platforms," he said.

A government spokesperson said it was preparing legislation to make it impossible for children to take, share or view nude images on their devices, which would make the UK the first country to do so.

"Alongside this, tech companies must be part of the solution and meet their legal and moral obligations. Where they fall short, the government will not hesitate to step in," the spokesperson said.

Kerry Smith, chief executive of the IWF, said: "We welcome the commitment to introducing nudity blocking technology on children's devices – but there really is no time to lose."

Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, said it is working to "fight and prevent grooming in a range of ways".

A Meta spokesperson said: "This includes restricting contact between adults and teens they're not connected to, and using technology to find and remove known child exploitation imagery.

"We also use behavioural signals to identify accounts showing possible signs of grooming or a sexual interest in children.

"Based on the strength of the signals, we either prevent them from finding and following teens or we remove their account completely."

articles.title: Helen Goh’s recipe for baked oats with morello cherries and almond | The sweet spot
articles.summary: This moreish, flapjack-style oaty bake, flavoured with maple syrup and dotted with sour cherries, works as well for dessert as it does for breakfast I’ve been making versions of these baked oats ever since discovering Heidi Swanson’s recipe in Super Natural Every Day . This is my favourite store-cupboard version, for when stone fruit and berries have slipped out of season. I love them here paired with almonds and coconut drinking milk (the light kind sold in cartons, not the rich tinned variety). articles.content:
This moreish, flapjack-style oaty bake, flavoured with maple syrup and dotted with sour cherries, works as well for dessert as it does for breakfast

I ’ve been making versions of these baked oats ever since discovering Heidi Swanson’s recipe in Super Natural Every Day . This is my favourite store-cupboard version, for when stone fruit and berries have slipped out of season. Morello cherries are a dark, tart variety of sour cherry, with an intensity of flavour and bright acidity that stand up particularly well to baking. I love them here paired with almonds and coconut drinking milk (the light kind sold in cartons, not the rich tinned variety). The cherries I use are whole fruit in syrup, which I drain and dot over the oats – they remain distinct while becoming deliciously jammy as they bake. Almost any fruit compote or jam will work here, though, so choose your favourite.

Jarred cherries come in many forms, so if yours is more like a compote or jam, simply add it in small teaspoonfuls instead.

30g unsalted butter , melted and cooled slightly, plus extra for greasing 210g jumbo rolled oats 1 tsp baking powder 1 tsp ground cinnamon ½ tsp fine sea salt 1 large egg 60ml maple syrup , plus extra to serve 500ml coconut drinking milk 1 tsp vanilla extract 100-120g morello cherries in syrup , drained, or cherry compote or jam 30g flaked almonds Icing sugar , for dusting (optional) Yoghurt or cream, to serve

Heat the oven to 195C (175C fan)/385F/gas 5½ and lightly grease a 26cm ovenproof dish that’s about 5-6cm deep – the oat mixture will form a fairly shallow layer.

Put the oats, baking powder, cinnamon and salt in a medium bowl, mix well, then tip into the greased dish. In a large jug, whisk the egg, maple syrup and melted butter, then add the coconut drinking milk and vanilla, and whisk again to combine. Pour this evenly over the oats, then gently press down any oats that remain dry.

Dot the drained cherries evenly over the oats. If using a thicker compote or jam, drop small teaspoonfuls over the surface, then use the tip of the spoon to drag each one out slightly, creating ripples rather than deep pools. Scatter over the flaked almonds.

Bake for about 30 minutes, until golden on top and just set in the centre. Leave to stand for five to 10 minutes before serving, dusted with icing sugar if you like, and with yoghurt or cream and a little extra maple syrup alongside.

articles.title: Experience: I rate benches
articles.summary: My Instagram page started as something to amuse my friends, but it took off – and led to me meeting Sophie, who is now my wife The idea came to me in summer 2019, when I finished studying at Swansea University. One day I went walking with friends around the beautiful Penllergare Valley woods. As they played Poohsticks, I sat on a bench and took in the view. I noticed that someone had left flowers on the bench. I wondered who had put them there, who they were for, and why they’d chosen this location. articles.content:
My Instagram page started as something to amuse my friends, but it took off – and led to me meeting Sophie, who is now my wife

T he idea came to me in summer 2019, when I finished studying at Swansea University. One day I went walking with friends around the beautiful Penllergare Valley woods. As they played Poohsticks, I sat on a bench and took in the view.

I noticed that someone had left flowers on the bench. I wondered who had put them there, who they were for, and why they’d chosen this location. By the time we reached the next bench along the route, I was deep in thought about all the people who had sat there before me.

Both benches had beautiful views, and my friends and I started comparing them. I joked that someone should start rating benches of the world. In the following days, I set up an Instagram account called RateThisBench and then posted a handful of reviews of benches near my family home in Bristol, mostly to amuse my friends.

At the end of the summer, I planned to close the account. But my dad, Chris, had become quite invested in it. It became our joint project; after dinner we’d go out for a walk and assess a bench.

I wasn’t interested in growing the account, but the page took off. I suddenly had hundreds of followers – I’m currently at about 27,500.

I decided to devise a proper rating system. I usually post a picture of me sitting on the bench, a brief description of the site, and a mark out of 10. Its mark depends on the location, whether there is an arm and backrest, and the quality of its base. I give extra marks to wooden benches, because I think they’re the nicest, and also for interesting plaques or dedications. My lowest-rated are always ugly metal ones in city centres, with armrests mid-bench. Some are unusual – one had an inbuilt USB charging port – but most are unremarkable. My favourites have a wooden back and a lovely view.

Before long, people started messaging me, asking me to review their favourite benches. I feel a bit bad if I don’t give them a high mark, but it’s just my opinion. One woman asked me to visit one that’s dedicated to her brother, who was also called Sam, and she thought I looked like him. She was thrilled when I posted a picture of me on his bench, even though I don’t think I awarded it a high mark.

My favourite message, however, was from a girl named Sophie. She contacted me when the page was taking off, and reviewed me as a reviewer. She gave me top marks, and it made me laugh. We started chatting; she lived near me and I asked her to dinner. We were three dates in when I saw a great bench and asked her to photograph me on it. She’s been photographing me on benches ever since.

I’ve now reviewed more than 300 benches. Most of them are in the south-west, but I also do reviews whenever I travel. Some people might think it’s a boring hobby, but there’s nothing boring about spending time outdoors and sitting with your own thoughts. I think that’s why so many people want to have a bench dedicated to their memory when they die – they’re a place to take a moment out of our busy lives, appreciate what’s around us and think for a while.

While I’ve sat on a lot of nice benches, I’d never awarded a perfect 10, because there’s always room for improvement. However, in June this year, I gave 10/10 to the bench I sat on after marrying Sophie. I’d previously rated it a 9/10. It’s in a churchyard a short walk from our home in Gloucestershire. We wanted to get married at that church, in part because of the bench – we’ve spent hours sitting there, talking about our dreams for the future. Sitting on the bench alongside my wife for the first time was an amazing moment that merited upgrading the score. Since posting our wedding photos, the vicar has told us they’ve had a surge in wedding bookings.

I briefly contemplated stopping the page after we got married – in a way, it felt as though it had reached a natural conclusion. However, I ended up reviewing a bench on our honeymoon in Mexico and decided to carry on. It’s probably something that will be with me for ever now. Life may be busy, but I don’t ever want to be too busy to enjoy five minutes sitting on a bench.

articles.title: AFL sanctions Lachie Cowan after Carlton player’s illicit drug use at house party
articles.summary: Blues defender apologises after ‘conduct unbecoming’ verdict Handed two-match ban and fined following off-season night out Carlton defender Lachie Cowan has received a “wake-up call” after being suspended for two matches for the use of an illicit substance during a night out last weekend. In addition to the ban, which will be served at the beginning of next season, Cowan was handed a $5,000 suspended fine along with a “notifiable adverse finding” under the AFL’s illicit drugs policy. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Carlton defender Lachie Cowan has received a “wake-up call” after being suspended for two matches for the use of an illicit substance during a night out last weekend.

In addition to the ban, which will be served at the beginning of next season, Cowan was handed a $5,000 suspended fine along with a “notifiable adverse finding” under the AFL’s illicit drugs policy.

The 21-year-old must also undertake further education on illicit substances and their effects.

But the AFL Players’ Association boss James Gallagher is concerned the sanction could “disincentivise” players from seeking medical treatment and “particularly in an emergency”.

A club statement on Sunday afternoon said Cowan had “received medical treatment and underwent observation, before being discharged a short time later”.

Blues teammate Will Hayward was also admitted to hospital on Sunday and required stitches to a minor cut to his head in what Carlton said were “separate circumstances”.

“I should never have put myself in such a vulnerable situation, I want to apologise for the impact my actions have had on my family and the football club,” Cowan said.

“I also want to thank the medical professionals who helped me on the night, the football club for their ongoing support and everyone who took the time to reach out and make sure I was OK.

“This is a wake-up call and I am just so grateful to now be in a position to learn from this.”

Guardian Australia reported on Sunday that Cowan and former Sydney player Hayward were part of a larger group that had been socialising on Saturday evening.

Ambulance Victoria said paramedics responded to an incident in South Yarra at about 5.15am on Sunday, with a man in his 20s taken by ambulance to the Alfred hospital in a stable condition.

The sanctions handed to Cowan come with the AFL’s new illicit drugs policy due to come into effect in January 2027.

All players will be hair tested upon their return to training in January, with readings going as far back as three to six months prior, while education sessions will be held at all clubs across November and December.

“AFL Players have a responsibility to themselves and their professional careers to uphold community expectations,” AFL chief operating officer Tom Harley said.

“They are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with the use of illicit substances. Lachlan admitted his mistake and understands he must be accountable for his actions.”

Carlton expressed their disappointment in a statement while committing to provide Cowan with wellbeing support.

“Most importantly we are thankful that Lachie is OK and received the medical attention he needed,” Carlton football boss Chris Davies said.

“We have been in regular contact with Lachie this week and he has taken ownership of his mistake. Lachie understands that it is his responsibility to ensure he makes better decisions moving forward.”

The AFLPA acknowledged the outcome of the AFL’s investigation but said it was “unacceptable” Cowan seeking medical attention had become a public matter.

“We don’t want players using illicit substances and that is why the Illicit Drugs Policy is so important, with its overarching purpose to change behaviour and minimise harm,” Gallagher said.

“However, it is contrary to this health and wellbeing model to sanction players after they have sought medical treatment, particularly in an emergency. As an industry, we need to encourage help-seeking behaviour, not penalise or disincentivise it.”

paragraphs: Carlton defender Lachie Cowan has received a “wake-up call” after being suspended for two matches for the use of an illicit substance during a night out last weekend.
In addition to the ban, which will be served at the beginning of next season, Cowan was handed a $5,000 suspended fine along with a “notifiable adverse finding” under the AFL’s illicit drugs policy.
The 21-year-old must also undertake further education on illicit substances and their effects.
But the AFL Players’ Association boss James Gallagher is concerned the sanction could “disincentivise” players from seeking medical treatment and “particularly in an emergency”.
A club statement on Sunday afternoon said Cowan had “received medical treatment and underwent observation, before being discharged a short time later”.
Blues teammate Will Hayward was also admitted to hospital on Sunday and required stitches to a minor cut to his head in what Carlton said were “separate circumstances”.
“I should never have put myself in such a vulnerable situation, I want to apologise for the impact my actions have had on my family and the football club,” Cowan said.
“I also want to thank the medical professionals who helped me on the night, the football club for their ongoing support and everyone who took the time to reach out and make sure I was OK.
“This is a wake-up call and I am just so grateful to now be in a position to learn from this.”
Guardian Australia reported on Sunday that Cowan and former Sydney player Hayward were part of a larger group that had been socialising on Saturday evening.
Ambulance Victoria said paramedics responded to an incident in South Yarra at about 5.15am on Sunday, with a man in his 20s taken by ambulance to the Alfred hospital in a stable condition.
The sanctions handed to Cowan come with the AFL’s new illicit drugs policy due to come into effect in January 2027.

All players will be hair tested upon their return to training in January, with readings going as far back as three to six months prior, while education sessions will be held at all clubs across November and December.
“AFL Players have a responsibility to themselves and their professional careers to uphold community expectations,” AFL chief operating officer Tom Harley said.
“They are well-educated when it comes to the harms associated with the use of illicit substances. Lachlan admitted his mistake and understands he must be accountable for his actions.”
Carlton expressed their disappointment in a statement while committing to provide Cowan with wellbeing support.
“Most importantly we are thankful that Lachie is OK and received the medical attention he needed,” Carlton football boss Chris Davies said.
“We have been in regular contact with Lachie this week and he has taken ownership of his mistake. Lachie understands that it is his responsibility to ensure he makes better decisions moving forward.”

articles.content:
The director of Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Jojo Rabbit turns Kazuo Ishiguro’s AI fable into a twee, tiresome tale of love and grief

T aika Waititi detonates an explosion of postmodern quirkiness and ironic dorkiness in this unbearably mannered, unspeakably acted film. It’s a slice of sentimental whimsy-futurism and non-satire, adapted by Waititi from the Kazuo Ishiguro novel, which winds up saying nothing substantial or meaningful (or funny) about artificial intelligence, love or grief. Klara and the Sun is soft-centred sci-fi-lite, simultaneously demanding we laugh at its (unfunny) humour and wipe away a tear at its pass-agg poignancy. With earlier films like Hunt for the Wilderpeople and Thor: Ragnarok, Waititi showed he can do comedy. But this, sadly, is closer to his notorious fey-Hitler fantasy Jojo Rabbit – misjudged and self-admiring.

In the world to come in an uncanny valley of the almost-real, families can buy “artificial friend” or AF robots for their kids. In terms of tech plausibility overall, incidentally, their status isn’t entirely clear: AF salesperson (Natasha Lyonne) says that the recent third world war has wiped out the internet. (This post-WW3 world looks in pretty good shape apart from that.) And these AF humanoids incidentally have a kind of purple blood called PEC-9 running through them which one character incidentally tells us is “highly flammable”. (Uh-oh. Quite the design fault.)

One such AF is teen girl Klara, played by Jenna Ortega as a ditsy, cutesy, supremely lovable innocent: a manic pixie dream robot – only nice – who is solar-powered and who therefore, in her adorable childlike robot way, worships the sun as a god. But Klara is an earlier, more rudimentary AF model, less sophisticated and robust apparently than the newer upgrades which run on Bluetooth as opposed to solar. (Is that really better?)

At all events, her flaws are presented as analogous to the vulnerabilities of the human teen who wants Klara; this is Josie (Mia Tharia), a 14-year-old genius-prodigy who has been expensively “lifted” into a super-IQ class via a new surgical procedure, but who is also very lonely and suffering from an unspecified illness. Her uptight mom is played by Amy Adams and the grumpy housekeeper Melania – whose appearance is the nearest the film comes to comedy – is played by Rachel House. Klara goes to live with her new family in their distant home in a weirdly dreamlike Midwest farming landscape from which the city can only be glimpsed distantly, like Oz. Klara becomes certain that the sun lives in the nearby barn above, from which she can see it rising every morning; what a sweetly naive belief. And so it goes on, to a twist ending that is as unsatisfying and contrived as everything that has gone before.

The thought of robots or replicant youngsters having real intelligence or real feelings is a difficult subject; Hirokazu Kore-eda came unstuck with the idea of robot child replacements in his recent film Sheep in the Box . Kogonada’s parable After Yang , about AI child robots, was a more interesting and persuasive movie. But this is a sentimental and laborious mess.

articles.title: ‘A powerful act of imagination and self-affirmation’: experts on how to start writing a book
articles.summary: Thinking about writing a book and doing it are two very different things – so how to get started and follow through? At some point in their lives, many people are confronted with a big question: what if I wrote a book? Writing a memoir, murder mystery or steamy romance is an accomplishment. Like running a marathon or successfully filing your taxes, it speaks to grit, determination and hours of research and effort. How to start meditating How to start weightlifting How to start budgeting How to start running Continue reading...
articles.content:
Thinking about writing a book and doing it are two very different things – so how to get started and follow through?

At some point in their lives, many people are confronted with a big question: what if I wrote a book?

Writing a memoir, murder mystery or steamy romance is an accomplishment. Like running a marathon or successfully filing your taxes, it speaks to grit, determination and hours of research and effort.

But thinking about writing a book and actually doing it are two very different things. According to a 2021 survey by ThriftBooks , more than half of respondents thought they had a good idea for a novel, but only 15% had started writing, and only 8% had finished.

“So many reasons”, says Jami Attenberg, bestselling author and founder of the annual writing project 1000 Words of Summer.

For some, it’s a necessary form of artistic expression. “They’re born writers, and this is how they communicate with the world,” Attenberg says.

For others, she says, there’s a story in them that’s dying to get out, and writing provides “that cathartic release”.

“Writing a book is a powerful act of imagination and self-affirmation,” says Marita Golden, novelist and co-founder of the Zora Neale Hurston/Richard Wright Foundation, which fosters and celebrates Black writers. “It is demanding, scary and the kind of personal challenge that many people find irresistible.”

That there are so many different reasons for so many different people is encouraging, Attenberg says: “It means people still read, love and value books.”

And yet, lots of people who talk about writing books don’t actually do it – or they start, and never finish. (For example, without naming any names: me.)

For a lot of people, “it’s difficult and they don’t know how to do it”, says novelist Christopher Moore. “Once you’ve written one, it’s difficult, but you know how to do it,” he adds.

Often, Golden says, aspiring writers are stopped by their own negative self-talk. Perhaps others have questioned their abilities, or they feel writing a book is only for “certain types of people”, she says.

Some fret that they won’t accomplish what they set out to do. “People fear that if they begin the process, they won’t complete it, and that will reinforce their insecurity or open them to criticism and judgment,” Golden says.

Read. While everyone’s writing process is different, experts agree one practice is non-negotiable: reading. A lot. This allows you to figure out what you like and don’t like, identify the different tools authors use, and get inspired.

“Figure out who your influences are, what kind of books you want to be writing, what genre, what length, what kind of vibe,” says Attenberg, adding that she starts every workday by reading someone else’s writing. “Literature, to me, is a big, beautiful, noisy conversation, and we can all learn from and be inspired by other people’s work.”

Figure out why you want to write. “Having something to say is important,” says Moore. Even if you’re not writing a polemic, Moore says, in the process of writing a book, you should regularly be asking yourself: “What am I saying here?”

“It doesn’t have to be profound,” he says. “It might be showing your unique perspective on a topic that’s been covered.”

Research. “Some kind of research is where I start,” says Moore. This is more than looking up dates and places, he explains – it is finding out “what has been written before on the subject I’m interested in”, and then “creating characters to carry the story”.

Set a start date. It’s easy to slip into a trap of endlessly preparing to write – telling yourself you’re just going to do a little more reading or add further detail to your outline before you start. To escape this, Moore suggests setting a start date. “On that date, I begin,” he says. Sometimes, all he writes that first day is a paragraph: “And that’s OK.”

Take a writing class. In addition to learning the basics of the craft, taking a writing class can help you meet other writers who can support you on your journey, Golden says.

Write yourself a letter. “Try to recall what your intentions were when you began this project,” Attenberg suggests. “Think about why it’s important to you to finish it. What would it mean for you to complete this project?”

Then, she says, set a reasonable but firm timeline for yourself and get going.

Write a scene. Even if it’s not in order, even if it’s a hundred pages from where you last stopped writing, “giving your characters a chance to talk to each other or make decisions will give you guidance for where to go next”, says Moore.

Don’t rewrite. “People get stopped because their expectation for themselves is too high,” says Moore. Allow yourself to write until you have a full first draft, and only then go back and edit. “Once you have a thing that vaguely resembles a book, you can always go back and shape and polish it until it’s what you want,” he says. “No one will ever know that, for a while, your masterpiece was absolute shit.”

articles.title: Street Fighter review – nostalgia only goes so far in junky fighting game movie
articles.summary: There are brief, simple pleasures in the inevitable new big screen take on the classic game but like the recent Mortal Kombat movies, it’s a largely incoherent mess We just had Resident Evil , Zach Cregger’s giddy, nasty, devilishly fun spin on Capcom’s popular zombie franchise. It gave us renewed hope (after Sonic the Hedgehog, The Last of Us and Fallout) that video game adaptations could be good, actually. But now here comes Street Fighter, a garish and incoherent mess that amuses in fits and starts but barely improves on the Mortal Kombat movies before it, crushing those hopes in its atomic suplex. articles.content:
There are brief, simple pleasures in the inevitable new big screen take on the classic game but like the recent Mortal Kombat movies, it’s a largely incoherent mess

W e just had Resident Evil , Zach Cregger’s giddy, nasty, devilishly fun spin on Capcom’s popular zombie franchise. It gave us renewed hope (after Sonic the Hedgehog, The Last of Us and Fallout) that video game adaptations could be good, actually.

But now here comes Street Fighter, a garish and incoherent mess that amuses in fits and starts but barely improves on the Mortal Kombat movies before it, crushing those hopes in its atomic suplex.

Fans certainly won’t mind. They’ve kept the box office’s life bar in the green for these one-on-one fighter adaptations going all the way back to the disastrous 1994 Street Fighter movie starring Jean-Claude Van Damme and his $10,000-a-week coke problem . They’ll happily tolerate how the new Street Fighter, like those Mortal Kombat movies, can barely string together a cohesive plot, which has clearly been pencilled in as an afterthought between rounds of combat in yet another tournament-style narrative. None of that will matter because they’re just here for the dopamine hits by way of nostalgia.

To that end, the movie exhaustively rolls out all the iconic characters and moves from the games – like Sumo warrior E Honda’s hundred-hand slap or military bro Guile’s flash kick – not to mention some at-times striking anime flashback sequences and a bevy of pop culture ephemera from its early-90s setting. Grainy, UHF quality MTV video segments show Ken (Noah Centineo) to be a self-destructive New Kids on the Block-era celebrity party boy with flashy blond curls, while the needle drops bring back bygone hits like MC Hammer’s 2 Legit 2 Quit and Montell Jordan’s This Is How We Do It.

It’s all about keeping us pampered in those fond memories from our pubescent childhoods, including bits that bring back the way us preteen boys ogled the 16-bit version of hypersexualized Chun-Li. She’s played in the movie by the lively and commanding Callina Liang, who enters the frame thighs first and unfortunately plays the only character tasked with a gratuitous slow-motion shower scene.

Liang doesn’t let that stuff drag down her performance, which is formidable, while her physicality during fight scenes is genuinely impressive. She’s one of the handful who bring some modest pleasures to the overcrowded mess. WWE wrestler Cody Rhodes, wearing a cartoonish trapezoid blond wig as Guile, is genuinely funny in the way he barks pleasantries and threats in equal measure. Indian movie star Vidyut Jammwal, who is trained in the ancient martial art Kalaripayattu, brings captivating authenticity and hypnotic movements to his all-too-brief scenes as yoga priest Dhalsim. Even controversial comic and manosphere podcaster Andrew Schulz gives a convincing performance worthy of an essay, playing Ken’s manager, who capitalizes on his bro’s brawn while coddling his wounded ego.

But the likable performances get buried in a movie that often feels like it was made on a six-button control pad. Street Fighter is a barrage of character introductions and story arcs lifted from the games and animated spin-offs, colliding into one another in a way that makes a relatively linear plot (it’s a freakin’ fight tournament!) confusing. Did Vega edit this with his Wolverine-like claw hands?

The movie’s most amusing fight arrives early, with Ken and Ryu (Andrew Koji) reunited in a hotel room after a years-long fallout, lured back together for a world championship tournament that the movie’s villain M Bison organized for nefarious purposes. Ken furiously takes wild swings at Ryu. Flying kicks miss the mark. Roundhouses hit nothing but air. Ryu quickly and calmly out-maneuvers, blocking with a pillow and then hilariously slipping the pillow below Ken’s head to catch his wipeout, or tiptoeing away from Ken while planted in a sofa seat. It’s a standout scene that really does feel like it belongs to another, smarter movie.

Elsewhere, during a matchup between Ken and boxer Balrog (played by rapper 50 Cent), Sakurai learns the right lessons from Martin Scorsese’s Raging Bull, quick cutting between flashy hits and slow-motion impacts, the sloppy mix of blood and drool flying from Ken’s mouth hanging in the air long enough to appreciate its viscosity.

And then there’s Liang’s Chun-Li, whose legwork delivers spectacular action, while her character tends to be the one dragging others down to earth with quick, frank, intermittently funny verbal jabs. She’s the grounded one, standing 10 toes down in purpose and principle. Whenever Ken or Ryu start emoting or waxing philosophical like Steven Seagal or Van Damme in those movies that inspire Street Fighter, Liang’s Chun-Li calls out in the most basic terms how stupid they sound.

There’s several knowing winks at the fans like this, guarding against criticism by owning up to how silly this all is, which would land better if the movie ever rose above the stuff it’s making fun of. Instead, Street Fighter is satisfied punching down on itself, and everything that’s cringe about the 90s, while happily being stuck there, in the past, so it could pretend that this is as good as it gets for video game adaptations.

Street Fighter is out in Australian cinemas now and in the UK and US on 16 October

But now here comes Street Fighter, a garish and incoherent mess that amuses in fits and starts but barely improves on the Mortal Kombat movies before it, crushing those hopes in its atomic suplex.

Fans certainly won’t mind. They’ve kept the box office’s life bar in the green for these one-on-one fighter adaptations going all the way back to the disastrous 1994 Street Fighter movie starring Jean-Claude Van Damme and his $10,000-a-week coke problem . They’ll happily tolerate how the new Street Fighter, like those Mortal Kombat movies, can barely string together a cohesive plot, which has clearly been pencilled in as an afterthought between rounds of combat in yet another tournament-style narrative. None of that will matter because they’re just here for the dopamine hits by way of nostalgia.

To that end, the movie exhaustively rolls out all the iconic characters and moves from the games – like Sumo warrior E Honda’s hundred-hand slap or military bro Guile’s flash kick – not to mention some at-times striking anime flashback sequences and a bevy of pop culture ephemera from its early-90s setting. Grainy, UHF quality MTV video segments show Ken (Noah Centineo) to be a self-destructive New Kids on the Block-era celebrity party boy with flashy blond curls, while the needle drops bring back bygone hits like MC Hammer’s 2 Legit 2 Quit and Montell Jordan’s This Is How We Do It.

It’s all about keeping us pampered in those fond memories from our pubescent childhoods, including bits that bring back the way us preteen boys ogled the 16-bit version of hypersexualized Chun-Li. She’s played in the movie by the lively and commanding Callina Liang, who enters the frame thighs first and unfortunately plays the only character tasked with a gratuitous slow-motion shower scene.

Liang doesn’t let that stuff drag down her performance, which is formidable, while her physicality during fight scenes is genuinely impressive. She’s one of the handful who bring some modest pleasures to the overcrowded mess. WWE wrestler Cody Rhodes, wearing a cartoonish trapezoid blond wig as Guile, is genuinely funny in the way he barks pleasantries and threats in equal measure. Indian movie star Vidyut Jammwal, who is trained in the ancient martial art Kalaripayattu, brings captivating authenticity and hypnotic movements to his all-too-brief scenes as yoga priest Dhalsim. Even controversial comic and manosphere podcaster Andrew Schulz gives a convincing performance worthy of an essay, playing Ken’s manager, who capitalizes on his bro’s brawn while coddling his wounded ego.

But the likable performances get buried in a movie that often feels like it was made on a six-button control pad. Street Fighter is a barrage of character introductions and story arcs lifted from the games and animated spin-offs, colliding into one another in a way that makes a relatively linear plot (it’s a freakin’ fight tournament!) confusing. Did Vega edit this with his Wolverine-like claw hands?

The movie’s most amusing fight arrives early, with Ken and Ryu (Andrew Koji) reunited in a hotel room after a years-long fallout, lured back together for a world championship tournament that the movie’s villain M Bison organized for nefarious purposes. Ken furiously takes wild swings at Ryu. Flying kicks miss the mark. Roundhouses hit nothing but air. Ryu quickly and calmly out-maneuvers, blocking with a pillow and then hilariously slipping the pillow below Ken’s head to catch his wipeout, or tiptoeing away from Ken while planted in a sofa seat. It’s a standout scene that really does feel like it belongs to another, smarter movie.

Elsewhere, during a matchup between Ken and boxer Balrog (played by rapper 50 Cent), Sakurai learns the right lessons from Martin Scorsese’s Raging Bull, quick cutting between flashy hits and slow-motion impacts, the sloppy mix of blood and drool flying from Ken’s mouth hanging in the air long enough to appreciate its viscosity.

And then there’s Liang’s Chun-Li, whose legwork delivers spectacular action, while her character tends to be the one dragging others down to earth with quick, frank, intermittently funny verbal jabs. She’s the grounded one, standing 10 toes down in purpose and principle. Whenever Ken or Ryu start emoting or waxing philosophical like Steven Seagal or Van Damme in those movies that inspire Street Fighter, Liang’s Chun-Li calls out in the most basic terms how stupid they sound.

There’s several knowing winks at the fans like this, guarding against criticism by owning up to how silly this all is, which would land better if the movie ever rose above the stuff it’s making fun of. Instead, Street Fighter is satisfied punching down on itself, and everything that’s cringe about the 90s, while happily being stuck there, in the past, so it could pretend that this is as good as it gets for video game adaptations.
Street Fighter is out in Australian cinemas now and in the UK and US on 16 October

articles.content:
Regents Park, London This year’s art fair is a jumble sale of mediocre paintings for the super-rich, while its Masters sibling hawks dinosaur skulls and sleazy 19th-century nudes. Welcome to the art market as its most grotesque

N aked people climb out of the earth and run around waving their arms and screaming, while someone with a bird’s head and wings plays the bagpipes. It’s my favourite artwork at this year’s Frieze but don’t go looking for this wildly imaginative outrage among the heaps of contemporary art at Frieze London. It’s a painting by a 16th-century follower of Hieronymus Bosch and is on view at Frieze Masters, the posher tent on the other side of Regent’s Park.

I’m sorry to say I was bored rigid in Frieze London. Many people attend, I imagine, hoping to be informed and excited by the newest, coolest art, but you’ll see more genuinely avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tent. There are endless paintings, none of which are much good, interspersed with photographs which tend to be a little better. The first thing here that held me at all was a two-metre-tall, inkjet print by Wolfgang Tillmans called Paul, nude, golf ball in which the naked Paul has his elbows on the floor and his close-cropped head bowed between them in apparent despair, while the white ball beside him eerily mirrors the pale flesh of his bony back. But it’s not new – it dates from 1994.

And, oh Lord, those paintings. There seem to be millions of them. And an elegant white marquee full of gallery booths along endless white corridors is a ghastly way of showing them, a dreadful way of seeing. It’s not as rewarding as visiting galleries which can be interesting spaces. Here, everything is crammed in, like a huge shop – the Selfridges of art.

Frieze, it is claimed, defines the new and finds the stars of tomorrow. But it’s obvious that it really serves the needs of sellers and the tastes of a certain kind of extremely wealthy consumer. This is most apparent on VIP day when I enter along with a host of tech bros, hedge-fund managers, retired hedge-fund managers, their children, and – is that George Osborne? – who were actually here to buy this stuff. At Frieze Masters, I was about to ask the price of an Anselm Kiefer work, matted vegetation clogging its surface, when an elderly couple beat me to it. They were genuinely interested in purchasing. The price was just shy of a million quid.

Things you can put on your wall are still the most collectible art. At Frieze Masters, you will find works by established modern “masters”, many of whom are deceased: a series of stained, graffiti-laden visual poems by Cy Twombly, a grey, bleak nude by Leon Kossoff. But at the contemporary fair, some of it is jumble sale standard. At Los Angeles’ Night Gallery booth, Wanda Koop’s Radiance-Together depicts two candles burning side by side in a blue and purple setting. Aw, cute. Who on earth would take this seriously? Another of its artists, Andy Woll, shows a row of lazily brushed mountain views that are just as vacuous. Meanwhile, at the appropriately named Grimm Gallery, Rosalind Nashashibi – better known for her films – exhibits a silly painting of lovers between flowery borders.

Now here’s something different – a row of white mineral-like growths, eerily lovely, enigmatically organic: they’re Helen Chadwick’s Piss Flowers, a chance to own examples of a modern classic by this tremendous artist who died in 1996. Why is she not over in Frieze Masters? And at the back of the Edel Assanti booth is Lonnie Holley’s assemblage of a water tap on a rusty pipe entwined with wire and two green bottles on a rough wooden plinth. It has the raw tang of real life. Holley, a musician and artist from Birmingham, Alabama who held me spellbound a couple of years ago when he showed how he can create beauty from a random piece of wire, is a true American great who stands out in this blandfest.

So do Tracey Emin, Waqas Khan, Do Ho Suh, Catherine Opie and Zanele Muholi – but in all honesty the success rate at Frieze London is about one in 10. That’s far too low for an event claiming to define the artistic zeitgeist.

Over at Frieze Masters, you’ve got the best certificate of quality there is: time. If something has value after 50, 500, or 68,000,000 years, it’s probably good. That 68m years is no exaggeration for here on sale is a triple-horned, fossilised Triceratops skull. Is this really going to end up as decoration in some rich dude’s house?

Let’s get it in perspective. To call this head “museum quality” is an understatement. The Natural History Museum does not own a Triceratops fossil of this perfection. Palaeontologists, as the Guardian recently reported , are worried that the fashion for dinosaur specimens among the ultra-rich is inflating prices and locking out museums. There are several such marvels being sold here.

Frieze Masters is more visually exciting than Frieze London. It’s fruitier, stranger. You can buy armour, silverware, Arabian carpets, the stuff a decadent aesthete might have surrounded themselves with in 1896. It makes you realise how conformist the contemporary fair is. At Frieze Masters, you can indulge your most perverse tastes – there are loads of sleazy, 19th-century nudes.

But if it is more interesting, it is also more disgusting. Stalls fetishise objects from the past, ripping them out of context to display them as brightly lit gewgaws: a manuscript page cut from its codex, a face mask off an ancient Egyptian coffin, a stone head of a priest from 2nd century AD Palmyra. These things belong in museums, but here they all are in the isolating spotlight of luxury and money.

This is a festival of capitalism run amok. I could say jokingly you might buy this or that but you won’t, unless you are a squillionaire, nor will I. What was it Andy Burnham was saying about the tyranny of neoliberalism? Here it distorts art in a delirious orgy of commodification.

The Colnaghi booth could have been designed as a Marxist exposé of the art market. African wooden carvings stand in front of a kitsch 1920 nude by Giacomo Grosso. The lavish view of the model’s bum as she lies on silks and the fact that she’s wearing high heels make it comically clear this is finely painted soft porn. The African art, made for religious purposes, is reduced to decor in front of this commodified body. John Berger, the radical critic who saw nude paintings and other forms of commodified art as playthings of western capitalism, might have said: told you so.

articles.title: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s AI-generated social media content: ‘I guess maybe he’s bored?’
articles.summary: The host discussed the president’s focus on AI-generated social media videos and cognitive tests With other hosts on holiday, Jimmy Kimmel checked in on Donald Trump ’s antics, online and off, with just three weeks to go until the US midterm elections . Continue reading...
articles.content:
The host discussed the president’s focus on AI-generated social media videos and cognitive tests

With other hosts on holiday, Jimmy Kimmel checked in on Donald Trump ’s antics, online and off, with just three weeks to go until the US midterm elections .

“We’re three weeks away from the midterm elections, and the president is laser-focused,” joked Jimmy Kimmel on Wednesday evening. In reality, the president “spent part of his afternoon yesterday posting videos of humans getting attacked by animals”, including a real clip of a man getting mauled to death by a tiger at a South Yorkshire zoo last week, after he scaled a fence and entered the enclosure.

“I’m sure the guy’s family was thrilled to see Trump having fun with it,” Kimmel continued. “But he needed it to set up this delightful AI video – I’m sorry, SI video – of himself wrestling and ultimately taming a tiger of his own.” In the AI-generated clip, Trump chases, tackles and eventually hugs a tiger. “The most unrealistic part of that video is him running,” Kimmel quipped.

“I guess maybe he’s bored?” he added. “How could you be president and be bored, I have no idea.”

Still, as congressional races heat up across the country, Trump resumed his preferred mode: on the campaign trail. The president held two rallies on Wednesday, in Arizona and Montana. “You know, it used to be when an 80-year-old traveled between Montana and Arizona, it was to beat their tuberculosis,” Kimmel joked.

“But if anyone was worried about his brain, don’t,” he added. “He’s good. He’s giving himself cognitive tests and he’s passing them with flying colors.”

Though no one was asking for it, Trump reassured attenders at his Arizona rally that he was continually acing a cognitive test in which the subject repeats a list of five words back to the doctor. He provided an example: “hat, hair, logo, white, black,” which he then repeated before claiming he “aced” the test.

“Sir, you aced this test you just made up,” Kimmel deadpanned. “This is the test you would give your grandfather after he fell off his stepladder.”

Later in his speech, Trump again boasted about his cognitive test abilities. “They say very few people can do it, and almost none can do them in order like that,” he said. “But I can, you know why? Because I’m a frickin’ genius, that’s why.”

“And if you believe that, then you will also believe I’m sending you $5,000 apiece,” Kimmel added. “Who wants to see a genius dance to the Village People, huh?”

articles.title: This dripless oil can is the prettiest thing in my kitchen – and surprisingly practical
articles.summary: Holcomb Studios’ tabletop oil can is the upgrade your snack time – and kitchen – needs Five reasons you need a fish spatula, even if you hate fish Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things If an unfortunate incident befell and I was somehow forced to repopulate my kitchenware , I’d be OK with all of it being gone with the exception of one item – the shiny little oil can I use almost every single day. In a life that is often more complicated than it needs to be, simple pleasures can’t be underrated, and this one is among the nicest. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Holcomb Studios’ tabletop oil can is the upgrade your snack time – and kitchen – needs

I f an unfortunate incident befell and I was somehow forced to repopulate my kitchenware , I’d be OK with all of it being gone with the exception of one item – the shiny little oil can I use almost every single day. In a life that is often more complicated than it needs to be, simple pleasures can’t be underrated, and this one is among the nicest.

If the Wizard of Oz’s Tin Man went to Design Within Reach for an upgrade , this oil can would be the result – a tall and sexy stainless steel vessel with a long, skinny spout and a delicate handle, pretty enough to keep out on the dining table. It comes from Holcomb Studio, a delightful new tableware brand out of the Pacific north-west, run by a father and daughter duo. The pair make elegant, beautiful and reasonably priced kitchen goods and I do own a fair amount of their stuff, but nothing really compares to the oil can.

The very tip of the spout itself is hand-sharpened, a fun design feature that is also very practical. Because it’s a little sharp to the touch, when you stop pouring and tilt the can back to its upright position, that little lip slices through the stream of oil, preventing unsightly and annoying dribbles and drips. I can confirm the vessel is indeed “dripless”, as the brand calls it, and the pour, steady.

Every detail is as thoughtful and considered as the spout. The opening at the top of the can is wide enough that you don’t need a funnel when you refill it. I was able to just upend a tin of Fat Gold olive oil (peppery, bright, spicy and worth the money) into this without much thought, which is more than I can say for the repurposed Graza squeeze bottle that holds the olive oil I cook with.

You can absolutely use this oil can when you’re cooking, of course, but the way it dispenses the oil is slower and more considered than the aforementioned Graza bottle or any other olive oil container I have used – I’m not reaching for this if I need to eyeball two tablespoons to throw in a pan. Instead, the oil can is a perfect tool for a nice little tableside flourish, drizzling a little dribble on my favorite snack – an ersatz parfait of Greek yogurt, sliced almonds, marmalade of your choosing and more flaky sea salt than you think looks right.

Because I eat this snack quite often and also foist it upon my sister when she visits, I’m using the oil can a lot. My kitchen is the farthest thing from fancy, which is perhaps why I care so much about the objects I use every day. Aside from my battered and beloved Zojirushi , the stuff I have amassed over the years is of decent to good quality and simply pleasing to use – the kind of stuff that makes even the most Quotidian meals and thrown-together bits feel like a little luxury.

paragraphs: Holcomb Studios’ tabletop oil can is the upgrade your snack time – and kitchen – needs

I f an unfortunate incident befell and I was somehow forced to repopulate my kitchenware , I’d be OK with all of it being gone with the exception of one item – the shiny little oil can I use almost every single day. In a life that is often more complicated than it needs to be, simple pleasures can’t be underrated, and this one is among the nicest.

If the Wizard of Oz’s Tin Man went to Design Within Reach for an upgrade , this oil can would be the result – a tall and sexy stainless steel vessel with a long, skinny spout and a delicate handle, pretty enough to keep out on the dining table. It comes from Holcomb Studio, a delightful new tableware brand out of the Pacific north-west, run by a father and daughter duo. The pair make elegant, beautiful and reasonably priced kitchen goods and I do own a fair amount of their stuff, but nothing really compares to the oil can.

The very tip of the spout itself is hand-sharpened, a fun design feature that is also very practical. Because it’s a little sharp to the touch, when you stop pouring and tilt the can back to its upright position, that little lip slices through the stream of oil, preventing unsightly and annoying dribbles and drips. I can confirm the vessel is indeed “dripless”, as the brand calls it, and the pour, steady.

Every detail is as thoughtful and considered as the spout. The opening at the top of the can is wide enough that you don’t need a funnel when you refill it. I was able to just upend a tin of Fat Gold olive oil (peppery, bright, spicy and worth the money) into this without much thought, which is more than I can say for the repurposed Graza squeeze bottle that holds the olive oil I cook with.

You can absolutely use this oil can when you’re cooking, of course, but the way it dispenses the oil is slower and more considered than the aforementioned Graza bottle or any other olive oil container I have used – I’m not reaching for this if I need to eyeball two tablespoons to throw in a pan. Instead, the oil can is a perfect tool for a nice little tableside flourish, drizzling a little dribble on my favorite snack – an ersatz parfait of Greek yogurt, sliced almonds, marmalade of your choosing and more flaky sea salt than you think looks right.

Because I eat this snack quite often and also foist it upon my sister when she visits, I’m using the oil can a lot. My kitchen is the farthest thing from fancy, which is perhaps why I care so much about the objects I use every day. Aside from my battered and beloved Zojirushi , the stuff I have amassed over the years is of decent to good quality and simply pleasing to use – the kind of stuff that makes even the most Quotidian meals and thrown-together bits feel like a little luxury.

articles.content:
Live action role play, or Larping, allows me to straddle two worlds with fellow weirdos – and enter a realm where death can be reversed and I’m a cashed-up bureaucrat

E very Friday night on a community sports field in Melbourne’s inner north, a few hundred nerds dress up in historical armour and attack each other with foam latex swords. It’s live action role play: turbocharged Dungeons & Dragons meets medieval re-enactment.

I’ve been Larping for seven years. It’s the biggest thing in my life outside of comedy, and the two scenes have a lot in common. Everyone’s broke. Everyone was bullied in high school. No one gets into Larp or standup if things are going well.

The biggest commonality is the gatekeeping. A crusted old comic in the corner of a greenroom gasps: “You’re a fan of standup, are you? Name three of Carl Barron’s best jokes.” His Larp counterpart, a polyamorous he/they in a top hat with a cog on it, twirls a cane: “So you like Warhammer Fantasy Battle? Name three spells an elven cleric can use in combat.” I’d like to see those two sit down and collectively name three women who feel safe around them.

Swordcraft Quest is one of the biggest events on Australia’s Larp calendar. Hundreds of players pitch tents in a rocky cattle paddock in Pomborneit, Victoria, to roleplay living in a medieval fantasy village for a week called Sudenburg. It’s fully in character and immersive, save for a few modern conveniences. Even the most fearsome warrior needs a Portaloo and a soy flat white.

You can be a noble paladin, a sage elven scholar or a tricksy halfling bard. But if you’re a real freak, like myself, you’ll spend the week as a fiscally conservative tax agent. This year I was appointed Master of Coin, responsible for overseeing the town’s finances. My parents are retired microeconomists and I was conceived on budget night of 1994, so perhaps it was inevitable.

Money works weirdly in Larp. Twelve copper to a silver, 20 silver to a gold. A copper is worth between $3 and $6 in “shadow currency” (Australian dollars or Aud, pronounced “Ow-dh”). Four coppers is an hour of unskilled labour; two gets you a coffee. You can’t cash them back in at the end of the game, so many of my Larp friends end up rich in coppers but live below the poverty line in the real world.

As an itinerant touring performer and freelance writer, a steady nine-to-five data-entry job handling huge amounts of cash was the ultimate fantasy. And I revelled in the brutal bureaucracy of it all. Each day I opened up the tax office, made players present their in-character documentation and declare their assets and then place a few of their precious copper coins into a box marked TAX OFFICE COFFERS – LOOTABLE ITEM.

Throughout the week, players produced elaborate disguises, fraudulent documents and even held me up at (fake foam) knife-point in fruitless attempts to steal the town’s hoard. Each of these heists was prenegotiated out of character. The final night of the event, someone simply broke into the tent and took the coins for real, which has since sparked a genuine out-of-character investigation.

Tongue lodged firmly in cheek, Larpers love to replicate real-world dilemmas with a dirtbag medieval slant. Dwarven miners extract obsidian from a poisonous seam with indentured goblin child labour. (Fracking.) The Town Council funnels tax funds to their allies. (Cronyism.) Senate meetings grind to a standstill over whether to let in refugees who might bring an undead horde. (Xenophobia.)

Sometimes Larp and real life collide and form something that is technically “make-believe” but resonates beyond role play. Last year, a terminally ill player called Silas* knew it would be their last event, so they held their own funeral. Wearing elf ears and tucked into a mechanised wheelchair beneath heavy blankets, Silas laughed as friends took turns to deliver eulogies. Afterwards, they married their long-term partner in the tavern with a real celebrant presiding. The ceremony was soundtracked by live bards and emceed by a hulking man called The Mad Mage. It was a strange day that straddled two worlds: our collectively imagined realm of Sudenburg, where death can be reversed through magic, and the bleak reality of Silas’ diagnosis.

Larp is a special interest that can verge into obsession. I’ve sunk thousands of dollars and hundreds of hours into it. My house is full to bursting with wool, linen and silk, plate armour, chain mail and a longbow. I have more Larp shoes than regular shoes, and my wardrobe is evenly split between the 21st, 16th and 14th centuries.

I’m not the only one with a Renaissance streak. Fantasy is having a massive cultural resurgence. We’ve gone from twee cottagecore to wenchcore, maidencore and castlecore. Chappell Roan wears chain mail armour and wields a sword on the red carpet.

Every second queer in Brunswick Anytime Fitness has a gothic blackletter tattoo. An old high school Facebook friend who manages a Dunkin’ Donuts posts about craving a “little hobbity life”. Gen Z have even co-opted the term “Larper” to mean poser or fraud. In a time of relentless AI slop, fast fashion and impending climate apocalypse, we turn to the past. Well, a reimagining of a reimagining of the past: an ahistorical slurry of Arthurian romance, pre-Raphaelite idealism and dreamy Y2K aesthetics.

The Ren Faire has become an ironically cool place for twentysomethings to gnaw a turkey leg and prance around in Shein princess costumes. Larp remains the domain of the weirdo, the loser and the pedant. That’s what makes it so special. It’s given me a chosen family, a community and – most importantly – the chance to go back in time for a week every year and pretend to be a cashed-up bureaucrat. Wouldn’t trade it for all the copper in Sudenburg.

articles.title: ‘Children are naturally drawn to beauty’: the head of the ‘Issey Miyake’ preschool on their pleated uniforms
articles.summary: Ms Lam Montessori’s head of school reveals teachers wear a different Japanese designer after their chic clothes drew online envy “Does anyone know what the deal is Ms Lam Montessori … and why all their employees wear Issey Miyake … every day … I’m confused and a bit jealous,” asked one commenter on the Williamsburg subreddit last week, sparking a unexpected viral moment for a chain of Brooklyn Montessori preschools. It seemed an avant-garde choice for staff posing in front of the abachi and blond wood toys of their preschool classroom. Continue reading...
articles.content:
Ms Lam Montessori’s head of school reveals teachers wear a different Japanese designer after their chic clothes drew online envy

“D oes anyone know what the deal is Ms Lam Montessori … and why all their employees wear Issey Miyake … every day … I’m confused and a bit jealous,” asked one commenter on the Williamsburg subreddit last week, sparking a unexpected viral moment for a chain of Brooklyn Montessori preschools.

The poster was responding to photos on the Montessori’s website of the teachers’ uniforms: raspberry, cobalt and apple green dresses in plissé fabric. They appeared to be from the Pleats Please line by Japanese designer Issey Miyake. It seemed an avant-garde choice for staff posing in front of the abachi and blond wood toys of their preschool classroom.

On X, those pictures were screen grabbed and viewed 3.5m times, with most comments reading along the lines of “only in Brooklyn”.

Over email from Taiwan, Ms Lam Montessori head of school, Stephanie Woo – a vision in chartreuse pleated fabric and matching hexagonal-framed glasses on the nursery’s website – explains that the dresses are actually by a more affordable Japanese designer, Yamasaki Takashi (they are priced around a 10th of the $700 one might pay for a Pleats Please frock), and are worn at all of the company’s locations. Ms Lam is a Mandarin immersion school and was originally founded in Taipei, Taiwan, where it has 14 branches, as well as its five in Brooklyn.

Woo is herself a “huge fan” of Issey Miyake, and owns “a couple of pieces that I bring out for special events at the school”. She adds: “Issey Miyake clothing is of course stunning, but we chose Yamasaki for its understated designs, comfort, durability and price. Those qualities made it a particularly good fit for everyday life in our classrooms,” she writes, adding that the clothes wash well and “hold their color and shape beautifully. Even after we’ve washed it 100 times, they still come out of the dryer looking much the same.”

She adds that the outfits were originally her mother’s idea – the original Ms Lam – who, according to the company’s website, was the first person to bring Montessori to Taiwan. Staff in Taiwan have been wearing them for 12 years and in Brooklyn for eight. Uniforms are important, she says, working with children from the age of one to six: “They help a young child recognize, even on a busy campus, this adult can help me.”

One of the reasons the Issey Miyake-esque outfits so delighted the internet is that the Pleats Please line, which launched in 1993, is having a fashion resurgence.

One particular garment – the Madame T stole, a large piece of plissé fabric with a diamond-shaped neck hole, which comes with an instruction booklet for the many ways it can be folded around the body – has recently become a social media fascination . In August, the shopping platform Lyst ranked it among the hottest products of the summer, and reported a 100% rise in demand for Issey Miyake quarter-on-quarter.

That said, Issey Miyake – which was launched in 1970 in Tokyo – and its more affordable Pleats Please line has never really been uncool. Miyake was the first of the wave of Japanese designers – followed by Yohji Yamamoto and Rei Kawakubo’s Comme des Garçons – to break through into European fashion.

Miyake developed his then revolutionary near-permanent pleats in the late 1980s, by constructing garments first, flat, at a much larger size than they would eventually fold down to, then heat-pleating afterwards. Most Pleats Please garments are 100% polyester, and their popularity comes despite a larger polyester backlash . Unlike fast-fashion polyester, Pleats Please are high quality, the designs timeless – and the construction of the garments makes specific use of polyester’s thermoplastic properties to hold shape, rather than using cheap polyester to make throwaway knockoffs of natural fibers.

Pleats Please’s practical, technical and arty associations – the focus is on the garment, and its own silhouette, rather than the body beneath – has made it popular with accomplished creative women for decades. Zaha Hadid, Solange Knowles, Meryl Streep, Tessa Thompson and Joni Mitchell are among its longtime fans, while Lorde, who wore a neon pink Pleats Please crop top at Lollapalooza Doja Cat have been spotted wearing the designer more recently.

In the west, says Dr Sasha Raspopina, the course leader for the fashion marketing and journalism BA at London Metropolitan University, Pleats Please has a kind of “if you know you know” appeal. She has noticed its adoption in east London among young people, who are perhaps “trying to signal that they are creative”. Given that context, Raspopina thought the Montessori image was a meme at first because the garment seemed to speak of an “alternate universe” to that of the kindergarten teacher.

The use of a Pleats Please-inspired garment may land differently for an east Asian audience, says Prof Wessie Ling, a visiting professor of transcultural arts and design at the University of Bologna (who, as a fashion scholar, knew the dresses weren’t genuine Miyake the moment she saw the photo: “the materials, and how it drapes on the body isn’t quite there,” she says).

She says that the link between Japanese design and Taiwan is very deep, given the colonial history (Taiwan was under Japanese colonial rule from 1895 until 1945). In east Asia more broadly, she says, there is a profound “admiration for Japanese designers, specifically the first generation of Japanese designers”. Miyake was the first to open a boutique in Paris, in the 1970s, nearly 10 years before Comme des Garçons and Yohji Yamamoto. This was at a time when “absolutely no other non-white designers made it into the fashion capital. So he represents something.” In east Asia, she says. Miyake is “the signature Japanese designer” and the first designer brand a woman would turn to if they reached executive level.

Ling had not heard of the brand Yamasaki Takashi , but she has noticed many younger, independent east Asian designers, including those based in South Korea and Vietnam, recently using pleats similar to Miyake’s. She doesn’t necessarily consider them to be copycats. “Obviously it is a kind of Miyake because it’s pleats – but they also create different patterns, colors and silhouettes, and they are putting some thought into the pleats they are trying to create.”

As Woo adds over email, the aesthetic of the garments certainly matters, even at school: “The truth is, we believe young children should be surrounded by beauty. From birth to age six, children have what Montessori calls the ‘Absorbent Mind’ – they effortlessly absorb so much from their surroundings,” she says. “They are naturally drawn to beauty, and by making it part of their daily lives, we hope to nurture their appreciation for it and their desire to care for the spaces and things around them.”
